thresholds.label: Up to $10,000 (ex GST)
thresholds.rule: A NSW Government agency may procure goods and services up to $10,000 (ex GST) from any supplier, even where the item is available on a whole-of-government arrangement. Purchases at this level should be made on a purchasing card (PCard) under the Faster Payment Terms Policy, subject to your agency's own PCard thresholds. You still need approval from a financial delegate, and you still need to record the value for money reasoning.

thresholds.label: Up to $50,000 direct from a small business
thresholds.rule: NSW Government agencies may purchase goods or services up to $50,000 directly from a small business, even where those goods or services are available on a whole-of-government arrangement. A small business for this purpose has fewer than 20 full-time equivalent employees.

thresholds.label: Up to $150,000 direct from a regional supplier
thresholds.rule: A NSW Government agency may buy directly from a regional supplier for procurements under $150,000.

thresholds.label: $150,000 (inc GST) - public contract disclosure
thresholds.rule: Under the Government Information (Public Access) Act 2009 you must publicly disclose contracts valued at $150,000 (inc GST) or more. Agencies disclose on NSW eTendering within 45 working days of the contract taking effect, and the entry stays listed for at least 20 days or until the contract is complete, whichever is longer. Councils maintain a public contracts register under section 27 of the GIPA Act on the same $150,000 (inc GST) trigger, entered in the register within 45 working days of the contract becoming effective and kept available for 20 working days or until contract obligations are satisfied, whichever is longer.

citations.label: IPC NSW - Register of government contracts

thresholds.label: Up to $250,000 - first consideration to Aboriginal business
thresholds.rule: Under the Aboriginal Procurement Policy, NSW Government agencies must give first consideration to Aboriginal businesses for procurements up to $250,000, and may buy directly from them, even where a mandated scheme or panel exists. An Aboriginal business for this purpose has at least 50 per cent Aboriginal ownership and is recognised through an appropriate organisation such as Supply Nation, the NSW Indigenous Chamber of Commerce, or the Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations.

thresholds.label: $250,000 (inc GST) - council tendering threshold
thresholds.rule: Section 55 of the Local Government Act 1993 requires a council to invite tenders before entering into a contract. Section 55(3)(n) exempts contracts involving estimated expenditure or receipt of less than $250,000. The OLG Procurement Guidelines confirm this threshold is INCLUSIVE of GST and applies to the total estimated contract value, which expressly includes cumulative expenditure with a supplier for similar goods and services. Councils must not invoice split or order split to avoid tendering, as that would be contrary to the Act. Procurements under the threshold are exempt from the legislated tendering requirements only - the principles in the Guidelines still apply at any value. This is a council rule and is entirely separate from the NSW Procurement Board thresholds that apply to state agencies.

citations.label: Procurement Guidelines for NSW Local Government (OLG, July 2026)

thresholds.label: $680,000 - unaccredited agency ceiling and EPP trigger
thresholds.rule: Two separate rules sit near this figure. First, an unaccredited NSW Government agency can generally procure goods and services not available on whole-of-government arrangements up to about $680,000; above that it needs concurrence on its procurement strategy from an accredited agency in its portfolio or from NSW Procurement. Second, the enforceable procurement provisions in PBD-2019-05 generally apply where the estimated value exceeds $680,000 (ex GST) for goods and services, or $9.584 million (ex GST) for construction.

thresholds.label: $3 million - SME first preference and mandatory non-price criteria
thresholds.rule: Under the SME and Regional Procurement Policy, agencies must give first preference to SMEs for direct procurements up to $3 million, including when buying from a prequalification scheme or panel. For contracts over $3 million the policy sets mandatory minimum non-price evaluation criteria; agencies may apply those criteria below the threshold as well. An SME is an Australian or New Zealand based enterprise with fewer than 200 full-time equivalent employees.

thresholds.label: $7.5 million - local market testing and shorter payment terms
thresholds.rule: For projects worth more than $7.5 million, agencies must engage with local NSW suppliers before going to tender and must embed upfront local market testing in the procurement plan under PBD-2024-02. Separately, large businesses holding NSW Government goods and services contracts over $7.5 million must pay small businesses they directly subcontract within 20 business days of a correctly rendered invoice, under the Small Business Shorter Payment Terms Policy; model contract clauses should be used for these contracts.

citations.label: PBD-2024-02 Increasing opportunities for local suppliers
Small Business Shorter Payment Terms Policy

thresholds.label: 5 business days - small business invoice payment
thresholds.rule: Correctly rendered invoices between $10,000 and $1 million from registered small businesses (fewer than 20 FTE) must be paid within 5 business days under the Faster Payment Terms Policy. Invoices under $10,000 should be paid as soon as possible, ideally instantly by PCard.

thresholds.label: Agency accreditation ceilings
thresholds.rule: Level 1 accredited agencies may procure goods and services not available on whole-of-government arrangements up to $50 million for low risk, $35 million for medium risk and $20 million for high risk procurements; above those values they need concurrence from a level 2 agency in their portfolio or from NSW Procurement. Level 2 accredited agencies may procure any value within budget and play a concurrence role for their portfolio. Unaccredited agencies are generally capped at about $680,000.

thresholds.label: $150,000 (inc GST) - council modern slavery reporting
thresholds.rule: Councils have been required to take reasonable steps to ensure goods and services they procure are not the product of modern slavery since 1 July 2022. From 1 July 2024, a council must file an online report with the Office of the NSW Anti-slavery Commissioner within 45 days of a contract taking effect where that contract arose from a heightened modern slavery due diligence process and is valued at $150,000 (inc GST) or more.

citations.label: OLG circular 23-17 - councils' obligations under the Modern Slavery Act

thresholds.label: 21 days - minimum council tender period
thresholds.rule: Under the Local Government (General) Regulation 2021, a council's tender deadline must be at least 21 days after the date the advertisement is first published. In selective tendering under clause 168, the same 21-day minimum applies again to the invitation to tender issued to shortlisted applicants.

thresholds.label: 25 days - recommended agency tender period
thresholds.rule: For NSW Government agencies, allow a minimum of 25 calendar days when you publish a tender on NSW eTendering. Ten calendar days is the minimum recommended where the procurement was published in your agency's annual procurement plan within the last 12 months, where you are buying through approved arrangements such as a prequalification scheme, or for recurring procurement arrangements. There is no set minimum for genuinely urgent or emergency procurements. Covered procurements over $680,000 have their own minimum tender periods under the EPP Direction.

thresholds.label: 5 years - normal maximum contract term
thresholds.rule: As a general rule you should not make a contract run longer than 5 years, including any extension options. Whole-of-government contracts typically run for 3 years with 1 or 2 year extension options.

glossary.definition: An ongoing NSW Procurement Board assessment that authorises a government agency to procure goods and services up to a set value. Level 2 is the highest. Councils are not accredited under this scheme.
An invoice that meets the requirements set out in the contract or purchase order, so payment clocks such as the 5-business-day Faster Payment Terms rule start running.

A procurement caught by the enforceable procurement provisions in PBD-2019-05, generally above $680,000 (ex GST) for goods and services or $9.584 million (ex GST) for construction, giving suppliers enforceable rights.
Expression of interest. A first-stage market approach that shortlists capable suppliers. No pricing and no contract award at this stage.
NSW Procurement Board Direction PBD-2019-05, which implements Australia's international trade agreement obligations in NSW procurement.
Government Information (Public Access) Act 2009. Creates a public right to government information and requires public disclosure of contracts of $150,000 (inc GST) or more.
Also called piggybacking. A procurement arrangement set up by one agency that other agencies are permitted to use.
Purchasing card. A government credit card used for low value purchases, typically under $10,000, which removes the need to raise a purchase order.
A list of suppliers assessed as capable in defined categories, sometimes called a procurement list. Using one streamlines a competitive process but does not by itself prove value for money.
Acting ethically, with integrity, uprightness and honesty. In procurement it means value for money, impartiality, consistency and fairness, and accountability and transparency.
A commercial document issued by a buyer to a seller. It becomes a legally binding contract once the seller accepts it. Often used where no standalone contract is issued.
Umbrella term for market approach documents: RFI, EOI, RFQ, RFP and RFT.

Small or medium enterprise. Under the SME and Regional Procurement Policy, an Australian or New Zealand based business with fewer than 200 full-time equivalent employees. Small is 1 to 19 FTE, medium is 20 to 199 FTE.
For the Faster Payment Terms Policy and the $50,000 direct purchase rule, a business with fewer than 20 full-time equivalent employees.
A proposal put to government that was not requested through a market approach. In NSW these must be referred to the Department of Premier and Cabinet.
Total lifetime benefit minus total lifetime cost. Not the lowest price and not the highest quality, but fit for purpose at the lowest whole-of-life cost.
A contract appointing one or more suppliers to supply any NSW Government agency, usually for 3 years with extension options. Agencies must generally use one where available unless exempt.

chunks.heading: The five NSW procurement objectives
chunks.summary: Five objectives guide all NSW Government procurement decisions.
chunks.text: The NSW Government has five key objectives which guide its procurement decisions. Value for money: ensuring best value for money in the procurement of goods, services and construction. Fair and open competition: improving outcomes for NSW by broadening access to government procurement. Easy to do business: being the easiest state to start and stay in business. Innovation: assisting government to work smarter and deliver better services. Economic development, social outcomes and sustainability: supporting economic participation and social outcomes, developing skills and creating jobs. Value for money is the main aim of procurement and should be your first consideration in every procurement.
checklist: Can you state, in one sentence, the value for money case for this purchase?
Have you done anything that narrows competition unnecessarily?
Is it easy for a small supplier to understand and respond to what you have written?
Have you looked for a better, faster or cheaper way of meeting the need?
Have you considered the social, economic and environmental effects of this spend?

chunks.heading: What value for money actually means
chunks.summary: Value for money equals total lifetime benefit minus total lifetime cost. It is not the lowest price.
chunks.text: Put simply, value for money equals the total lifetime benefit minus the total lifetime cost. Value for money is the main aim of procurement and your procurement decisions and outcomes must reflect it. Value for money is not necessarily the lowest price, nor the highest quality good or service. Generally you achieve value for money by buying fit for purpose goods or services at the lowest lifetime cost. When assessing value for money, consider the range of cost-related and non-cost factors, both up-front and after the initial purchase. Fit for purpose is about whether the goods or services will meet the business need, and is generally determined by non-cost factors. Determining whether goods are fit for purpose is often easier because goods are tangible. When assessing services, consider suppliers' capability and capacity. Capability means the supplier can perform the service - the right skills, qualifications, experience, licences and insurances. Capacity means the supplier can actually deliver - sufficient time, sufficient staff, the right equipment, the right materials and other required resources.
checklist: List the up-front costs and the ongoing costs over the whole life of the arrangement
Identify the non-cost factors that determine fitness for purpose
Test capability: skills, qualifications, experience, licences, insurances
Test capacity: time, staff, equipment, materials, other resources
Record the value for money reasoning, even for a small purchase
watch_outs: Choosing the cheapest bid without a fitness-for-purpose assessment is not value for money and is hard to defend later
A supplier can be capable but not have the capacity to take on your work right now - test both

chunks.heading: Fair and open competition
chunks.summary: Competition delivers savings, quality and innovation. Avoid behaviours that quietly shut it down.
chunks.text: Competition helps to deliver outcomes such as cost savings, increased quality and innovation and improved market sustainability. Competition exists where suppliers are under pressure to offer the best possible range of goods and services at the best possible prices. To help promote fairness and open competition you should especially encourage new businesses, including local suppliers, SMEs and gender-equitable suppliers, to compete for government work; make your processes simple and transparent; break down silos within your agency and government to share ideas for procurement; and avoid behaviours that limit competition, including being overly prescriptive and not questioning the status quo.
watch_outs: Writing a specification around the incumbent's product is a common and serious way of killing competition
Repeating last cycle's requirements without questioning them entrenches the status quo

chunks.heading: Easy to do business and faster supplier payments
chunks.summary: Keep contracts short and plain, give suppliers notice, and pay promptly - cashflow is critical to small business.
chunks.text: The NSW Government wants to attract a broad supply base that includes local businesses, small and medium enterprises, regional, gender equitable and Aboriginal businesses, with the aim of making NSW the easiest state in which to do business. To help achieve this you should use eTendering or your agency's procurement system to make suppliers aware of contracting opportunities in advance and give them time to prepare; make it easy for suppliers to understand and comply with contractual terms by keeping contracts brief, in plain English and including only necessary conditions and insurances; and pay promptly, because cashflow is vital to small businesses. On payment: pay correctly rendered invoices up to $10,000 instantly via your agency's purchasing card, subject to your agency's rules and PCard thresholds; and pay correctly rendered invoices between $10,000 and $1 million within 5 business days if the supplier is a registered small business, as per the Faster Payment Terms Policy.
checklist: Advertise upcoming opportunities early so suppliers can prepare
Strip the contract back to necessary conditions and insurances only
Confirm the supplier's small business registration status so the 5-day clock applies correctly
Use a PCard for purchases under $10,000 where your agency allows it
Check what makes an invoice 'correctly rendered' - the clock does not start until it is

chunks.heading: Innovation and unsolicited proposals
chunks.summary: Engage the market early to open up innovation. Unsolicited proposals must go to Premier and Cabinet.
chunks.text: You can deliver better outcomes for the government and citizens of NSW by being innovative with your procurement. This could be in your procurement approach, in designing your requirements, the outcome you are seeking, or the way you deliver the outcome. One way to increase opportunities for innovation is by engaging suppliers early and in an ongoing way. You should look for suppliers who can deliver new, faster, more cost-effective and better goods and services, and look to innovate at every stage of the procurement process, especially when you engage with industry and approach the market. Unsolicited proposals can often be a good source of innovation, but they are also risky. For this reason you must refer unsolicited proposals to the Department of Premier and Cabinet.
watch_outs: Do not deal with an unsolicited proposal yourself - it must be referred to the Department of Premier and Cabinet

chunks.heading: Economic development, social outcomes and sustainability
chunks.summary: Sustainable procurement means weighing the effects of the purchase on society, the economy and the environment.
chunks.text: Considering benefits and impacts on society, the economy and the environment in your procurement is called sustainable procurement. Examples include encouraging skills development; creating jobs for the citizens of NSW; encouraging supplier diversity and increasing opportunities for minority businesses such as SMEs, regional businesses, Aboriginal businesses and disability employment organisations; complying with fair trade, human rights and modern slavery legislation; pollution control, waste minimisation, recycling and disposal; and energy efficiency and resource consumption. The Guide to Environmentally Sustainable Procurement includes practical templates and case studies from NSW Government agencies and covers the planning, sourcing and managing stages.

chunks.heading: When you must preference certain suppliers
chunks.summary: Aboriginal businesses get first consideration up to $250,000; SMEs get first preference up to $3 million - even off a panel.
chunks.text: There are times you must give preference to buying from certain suppliers, particularly SMEs, Aboriginal businesses and local suppliers. This applies even when you are buying from a standing offer, panel or prequalification scheme. SMEs may include Aboriginal businesses, regional businesses, social enterprises and disability employment organisations. The Aboriginal Procurement Policy requires that you give first consideration to Aboriginal businesses for procurements up to $250,000. The SME and Regional Procurement Policy extends the direct purchasing preference threshold to $3 million. When deciding which policy to apply, consider the market, your agency's requirements and NSW Government targets for direct spend with Aboriginal businesses. You are also encouraged to buy from social enterprises to support economic and social change for disadvantaged people. Social enterprises tackle social problems, improve communities, provide people with access to employment and training, or help the environment; many are small businesses, SMEs, Aboriginal businesses or Australian Disability Enterprises and qualify for purchasing preferences. The NSW Government is also committed to improving gender equality in supply chains.
checklist: Before you approach the market, check whether an Aboriginal business can meet the need (mandatory first consideration up to $250,000)
For direct purchases up to $3 million, check SME options first - including when buying off a panel
Search the Supplier Hub for verified Aboriginal, social enterprise, disability employment and gender equitable identifiers
Record why you did or did not use a preferenced supplier

chunks.heading: The Procurement Policy Framework
chunks.summary: The single source of guidance on NSW procurement objectives, Board requirements and rules. Updated quarterly.
chunks.text: The Procurement Policy Framework is your single source of guidance on government procurement objectives, Board requirements and rules for procurement in the NSW public sector. It includes mandatory rules based on legislation, Board Directions and policies, plus guidance on good practice with supporting documents. It is updated every three months with new and revised requirements. It has four sections: Section 1 Objectives, covering the goals of NSW Government procurement and supporting policies; Section 2 Plan, source, manage process, the best practice approach with relevant policies highlighted at each stage; Section 3 Governance and feedback, the structures supporting NSW Government procurement; and Section 4 Glossary. The Framework uses two key terms. MUST shows rules that are mandatory as per legislation and policy. SHOULD, MAY and RECOMMENDED indicate good practice.
watch_outs: The Framework is reissued quarterly - check you are reading the current version before relying on a threshold or rule
'Must' means mandatory. 'Should' means good practice. Confusing the two is how audit findings happen.

chunks.heading: Public Works and Procurement Act 1912 and Regulation
chunks.summary: The Act that establishes NSW procurement, creates the Procurement Board, and sets agency obligations under section 176.
chunks.text: The Public Works and Procurement (PWP) Act 1912 establishes the legislative framework for the procurement of goods and services across the NSW public sector. Section 176 of the Act defines the obligations of government agencies, including obtaining value for money and exercising their procurement in accordance with the policies and directions of the NSW Procurement Board, the terms of their accreditation, and principles of probity and fairness. The Public Works and Procurement Regulation 2019 supports the Act and deals with specific procurement arrangements, including procurement for emergencies, purchasing from approved disability employment organisations, and procurement by public bodies that are not NSW Government agencies, such as councils, private schools and hospitals, universities and government agencies in other states or territories.

chunks.heading: ICAC Act, GIPA Act, State Records Act and Modern Slavery Act
chunks.summary: Four Acts that shape day-to-day procurement conduct: corruption, information access, recordkeeping and modern slavery.
chunks.text: The Independent Commission Against Corruption Act 1988 sets out the functions of the ICAC: to investigate and expose corrupt conduct in the NSW public sector, actively prevent corruption through advice and assistance, and educate the NSW community and public sector about corruption and its effects. The Act requires your agency head to report to the Commission any matter they suspect on reasonable grounds concerns or may concern corrupt conduct. The Government Information (Public Access) Act 2009 helps ensure an open and transparent government and provides the public with a right to government information. It requires that you publicly disclose contracts valued at $150,000 (inc GST) and over, and proactively share information about procurement processes and decision making. The State Records Act 1998 requires that you keep appropriate records of procurement planning, management and decision making, stored securely to maintain confidentiality, kept for audit purposes, and able to be extracted, collated and arranged for reports. The NSW Modern Slavery Act 2018 includes requirements to take reasonable steps to ensure the goods and services you procure are not the product of modern slavery, including annual reporting requirements. Procurement is also subject to a financial framework including the Government Sector Finance Act 2018, Treasurer's Directions, agency delegations and internal expenditure policies.

chunks.heading: Board Directions, procurement policies and agency policies
chunks.summary: Four layers of policy sit above your procurement: Board Directions, government policies, agency policy, and administrative requirements.
chunks.text: The NSW Procurement Board issues Board Directions to individual or all government agencies that set rules and guidelines around procurement. Examples include Directions that increase opportunities for local suppliers to supply to government, support bushfire and flood affected communities, enforce government procurement obligations arising from international procurement arrangements, define approved procurement arrangements for specific procurement values, and define arrangements for buying professional services. The Government, or the Procurement Board acting on its behalf, also issues policies that affect how you conduct procurement, including the SME and Regional Procurement Policy, the Aboriginal Procurement Policy, the Small Business Shorter Payment Terms Policy, and the Net Zero Government Operations Policy. Your agency procurement function will also have specific policies and procedures you must follow, usually set out in an agency procurement manual. The Government regularly issues further guidance collectively called Administrative Requirements, including Premier's Memoranda, Treasurer's Directions and Departmental Circulars.

chunks.heading: Enforceable procurement provisions and international trade agreements
chunks.summary: Above roughly $680,000 for goods and services, international trade obligations become legally enforceable by suppliers.
chunks.text: Australia is party to several international trade and procurement agreements that impact NSW Government procurement, including the Australia-United States Free Trade Agreement, the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, the World Trade Organisation Government Procurement Agreement, and the Australia New Zealand Government Procurement Agreement. Board Direction PBD-2019-05 Enforceable Procurement Provisions (the EPP Direction) implements the requirements of these agreements. Before starting your procurement process you must assess whether the procurement is covered by the EPP Direction. You generally need to comply if the estimated value exceeds $680,000 (ex GST) for goods and services, or $9.584 million (ex GST) for construction. Key consequences of a covered procurement include a general requirement to use an open approach to market, a prohibition on discriminating against foreign suppliers or requiring Australian experience, and specific minimum tender periods. Under the Public Works and Procurement Act 1912 a supplier may lodge a complaint with the head of a government agency alleging the agency has contravened an enforceable procurement provision, and the agency head must investigate and attempt to resolve it. The NSW Procurement Board has no statutory role in covered procurement complaints - they are a matter for the agency, the supplier and, if proceedings are taken, the Supreme Court.
checklist: Estimate the value of the whole procurement, including options and extensions, before deciding if the EPP Direction applies
If covered, default to an open approach to market
Remove any requirement for Australian experience or local presence that is not genuinely essential
Apply the EPP minimum tender periods, not just the general 25-day guidance
Document your covered-procurement assessment - it is the first thing a complaint will test
watch_outs: Splitting a procurement to fall under the threshold is a serious compliance failure
A covered procurement complaint can end up in the Supreme Court, not just in an internal review

chunks.heading: When you are exempt from some procurement policies
chunks.summary: Four situations where NSW procurement policies, including Board Directions, may not apply - but value for money always does.
chunks.text: Sometimes you do not have to comply with NSW Government procurement policies, including Board Directions. This includes buying from an approved Australian Disability Enterprise; emergency procurements; procurements approved by Cabinet or the Expenditure Review Committee; and buying from other government entities. Where a procurement is approved by Cabinet or the ERC you still need to comply with the Procurement Policy Framework and Board Directions where consistent with the Cabinet decision, including the need to achieve value for money, and you will still need to comply with PBD-2019-05 Enforceable Procurement Provisions.
watch_outs: An exemption from a policy is not an exemption from value for money, probity or recordkeeping
Even a Cabinet-approved procurement must still meet the enforceable procurement provisions

chunks.heading: Guidance on modern slavery, sustainability, accessibility and local suppliers
chunks.summary: Four guidance documents that operationalise the government's broader procurement objectives.
chunks.text: Several guides help you achieve the government's objectives relating to modern slavery, environmental sustainability, accessibility and engaging local suppliers. The NSW Anti-slavery Commissioner's Guidance on Reasonable Steps to Manage Modern Slavery Risks in Operations and Supply Chains aims to help agencies take reasonable steps to ensure goods and services procured by and for the agency are not the product of modern slavery; it became operative on 1 January 2024 and covers NSW government departments, local councils, certain universities, Local Aboriginal Land Councils and other state government agencies. The Guide to Environmentally Sustainable Procurement helps you increase environmental sustainability across planning, sourcing and managing. The Guidance on buying accessible products and services covers buying products and services usable by everyone, including people with disability. The Guidance on increasing opportunities for local suppliers sets out the rules on engaging local suppliers and the requirements for local market testing.

citations.label: Guidance on buying accessible products and services

chunks.heading: Devolved governance and the NSW Procurement Board
chunks.summary: The Board sets the system-wide rules; agency heads remain responsible for their own agency's procurement.
chunks.text: In NSW, government procurement operates within a devolved governance structure, governed by the NSW Procurement Board. The Public Works and Procurement Act establishes the Board. It is made up of heads of NSW Government departments, or their appointed deputies, and is chaired by the Deputy Secretary Commercial within NSW Treasury. The Board is responsible for the government-wide strategic approach to procurement and overseeing the procurement system, developing and issuing Board Directions and procurement policies, monitoring compliance, and investigating and dealing with procurement-related complaints. Your agency head is ultimately responsible for your agency's procurement; they enter into procurement agreements on behalf of your agency and make sure you comply with the NSW Procurement Policy Framework. An agency can also be responsible for a whole-of-government procurement arrangement, in which case it enters agreements on behalf of the whole of NSW Government. Agency heads typically delegate responsibility for procurement, often to a Chief Procurement Officer, and when doing so must ensure appropriate governance mechanisms are in place. CPOs prepare Agency Procurement Plans and Annual Outcomes Reports and review individual project or category procurement strategies. NSW Treasury manages several whole-of-government contracts and is responsible for centralised functions including agency accreditation, whole-of-government procurement policy, data collection and reporting, procurement advisory services, complaint and feedback mechanisms, and sector-wide capability development. Also critical to governance are the ICAC and the Audit Office of NSW, portfolio and agency governance functions, appropriate delegation of authority, effective procurement planning, purchasing and procurement systems, and efficient approval processes.

chunks.heading: Procurement Board subcommittees
chunks.summary: Four subcommittees: the Procurement Leadership Group, Risk and Compliance, Construction Leadership and ICT & Digital Leadership.
chunks.text: The Procurement Leadership Group (PLG) is the principal advisory group to the Board. It delivers state priorities by executing the government's and the Board's procurement objectives, and considers and advises on whole-of-government procurement strategy, financial performance, practices, policies and guidelines, resource and capability planning, and the innovation plan. The Risk and Compliance Subcommittee (RCS) reports on operational and administrative functions including Goods and Services Accreditation attestation and assurance outcomes, emergency procurement reported to the Board, ICAC reports and recommendations, NSW Audit Office reports and recommendations, supplier complaints to the Board, and remedial action for poor supplier performance or behaviour. The Construction Leadership Group (CLG) drives reform in the development, procurement and delivery of infrastructure and building projects, including procuring and managing projects more collaboratively, developing a transparent pipeline of projects, improving skills and training, reducing the cost of bidding, and improving the security and timeliness of contract payments. The ICT & Digital Leadership Group (IDLG) is the primary governance forum for ICT decisions and work programs across NSW Government, overseeing ICT strategies and policies, advising on investments under the ICT Assurance Framework, and driving cross-cluster expertise sharing.

chunks.heading: Agency accreditation levels
chunks.summary: Your agency's accreditation level caps the value of goods and services you can procure outside whole-of-government arrangements.
chunks.text: The NSW Procurement Board has established and governs the accreditation programs for goods and services procurement. Accreditation is an ongoing assessment process to authorise agencies to procure goods and services up to a certain value. Your agency's accreditation status determines the maximum value of goods and services you can procure. There are two levels; the highest is level 2. Level 1 accredited agencies can procure goods and services that are not available on whole-of-government procurement arrangements up to different maximum values depending on risk: low risk up to $50 million, medium risk up to $35 million, high risk up to $20 million. Above these thresholds they must seek concurrence on the procurement strategy from a level 2 accredited agency in their portfolio, or from NSW Procurement. Level 2 accredited agencies can procure goods and services of any value within their budget and play a leadership and concurrence role within their portfolio. If your agency is not accredited you can still procure goods and services not available on whole-of-government arrangements up to a certain value, usually $680,000; above that you need concurrence to your procurement strategy from an accredited agency in your portfolio or from NSW Procurement. Accreditation means an agency has proven it can meet minimum standards for effectively managing risk, driving continuous improvement in its procurement function, and delivering outcomes that provide value and match strategic priorities. Councils are not part of this accreditation scheme.
checklist: Look up your agency's current accreditation level and status on buy.nsw
Assess the risk rating of the procurement, not just its value - the ceiling changes with risk
If you are above your ceiling, start the concurrence conversation early; it takes time
Confirm you also have the financial delegation to approve the spend - accreditation and delegation are different things

chunks.heading: Government procurement arrangements: what you must use
chunks.summary: Work down the ladder: under $10,000 anywhere; then whole-of-government contracts; then schemes; then agency contracts; then the open market.
chunks.text: When planning a procurement you need to consider the buying solutions available, including existing government procurement arrangements. Board Direction PBD-2021-04 specifies the approved procurement arrangements for agencies. Under $10,000 (ex GST) you can procure from any supplier, even if the item is available on a whole-of-government arrangement, provided you get approval from someone with financial delegation, check and follow any additional agency rules, and keep records about your decisions and value for money assessment. Purchases up to $10,000 should normally be made using a purchasing card. Agencies may also purchase goods or services up to $50,000 directly from a small business, defined as fewer than twenty full-time equivalent employees, even where those are available on a whole-of-government arrangement. NSW Government contracts are the main way agencies buy goods and services: the general rule is that you must use a whole-of-government contract when one is available, unless you are exempt. A whole-of-government contract appoints one or more suppliers to supply any government agency and runs for a specific period, usually 3 years, with some having 1 or 2-year extension options. Example contracts include Facilities Management - Cleaning Services, Food Services, Office and Education Furniture, the Microsoft Enterprise Agreement, Telecommunications Purchasing Arrangements, Travel Management Services and Waste Management. You can also use prequalification schemes, sometimes called procurement lists, to choose prequalified suppliers based on categories or capabilities; suppliers go through an assessment process to join, and some schemes are mandatory while others are recommended. Examples include Contingent Workforce, ICT Services, Motor Vehicles, the Legal Services Panel and Performance and Management Services. Schemes do not generally include pricing information, so you still need to confirm you are getting value for money. Many agencies have their own contracts and prequalification schemes, and if your agency or portfolio has an existing contract you may be required to use it. Multi-agency access contracts, often called piggybacking contracts, are arrangements set up by one agency that other agencies can use, reducing market approaches and delivering volume savings. If nothing exists, first check whether your agency or portfolio is bound by any standing offers or panel contracts, then select an appropriate way to approach the market as per PBD-2021-04 and the terms of your agency's accreditation.
checklist: Is it under $10,000? Buy from anywhere, on PCard, with delegate approval and a recorded VFM note
Is it under $50,000 and from a small business? You can buy direct even if a WoG contract covers it
Is there a whole-of-government contract? If yes, use it unless you have a documented exemption
Is there a mandatory prequalification scheme for this category?
Does your agency or portfolio have its own contract you are required to use?
Could you piggyback on another agency's multi-agency access contract?
Only then design a fresh market approach

chunks.heading: Exemptions that let you buy direct
chunks.summary: Value and supplier-type exemptions that release you from using a whole-of-government arrangement.
chunks.text: The general rule is that you must use whole-of-government contracts or prequalification schemes, but there are exemptions. Your procurement may qualify due to the size or nature of the procurement or the supplier you choose. Where an exemption applies you can often buy directly from a supplier, but you should still make sure you are achieving value for money, for example by confirming quoted prices reflect market rates. Exemptions by value include: less than $10,000, buy directly from any supplier; less than $150,000, buy directly from a regional supplier; less than $250,000, buy directly from an Aboriginal business recognised through an appropriate organisation, or from a small or medium enterprise, and you can also buy ICT directly from an SME. There is no limit on buying goods and services from approved disability employment organisations via a single written quote. Note that NSW Government agencies must engage with local NSW suppliers before going to tender for projects worth more than $7.5 million.
keywords: buy ict directly from an sme

chunks.heading: Does a mandatory scheme override a direct-purchase exemption?
chunks.summary: The exemptions ARE exemptions from the mandate to use whole-of-government contracts and prequalification schemes, so a qualifying direct purchase does not need the supplier to be on the scheme.
chunks.text: This is the question people get wrong most often, because the two rules look like they contradict each other. They do not, and the order matters. The general rule is that you must use a whole-of-government contract or a prequalification scheme when one is available. The exemptions sit directly on top of that rule: the Procurement Policy Framework introduces them as exemptions FROM using government procurement arrangements, and states that where your procurement qualifies for an exemption you can often buy directly from a supplier. So a mandatory scheme does not defeat an exemption you actually qualify for - the exemption is what releases you from the scheme in the first place. Worked through for the common case: a procurement under $250,000 from a small or medium enterprise qualifies for direct purchase, and the Framework separately confirms you can buy ICT directly from an SME. On that basis an agency buying a $120,000 software solution from an SME is within the direct-purchase exemption, and the supplier does not need to be prequalified on the ICT Services Scheme for that purchase. The supplier preferencing rules point the same way rather than against it: the SME and Regional Procurement Policy requires first preference to SMEs for direct procurements up to $3 million, and says explicitly that this applies even when you are buying from a standing offer, panel or prequalification scheme. Three things still bind you. First, you must genuinely qualify - confirm the supplier meets the SME definition (an Australian or New Zealand enterprise with fewer than 200 full-time equivalent employees) and that your value estimate covers the whole contract including options. Second, an exemption removes the obligation to use the arrangement, not the obligation to achieve and evidence value for money, so test the price against the market. Third, individual Board Directions can attach their own conditions to a specific scheme, and your agency's own procurement policy may be stricter than the Framework - both bind you even where the Framework would allow the direct purchase. Check the current Board Direction for the scheme concerned and your agency's procurement team before relying on this.
keywords: must the supplier be on the scheme
checklist: Confirm the supplier genuinely meets the SME definition: an Australian or New Zealand enterprise with fewer than 200 full-time equivalent employees
Estimate the whole contract value including options and extensions, and check it sits under the exemption threshold
Identify the specific exemption you are relying on, and record it on the file
Check the current Board Direction for the scheme concerned in case it attaches its own conditions
Check your agency's own procurement policy, which may be stricter than the Framework
Test the price against the market anyway - an exemption does not remove the value for money obligation
Record the value for money assessment and the reason for the direct purchase
watch_outs: An exemption releases you from using the arrangement; it never releases you from value for money, probity or recordkeeping
Splitting a procurement so it fits under an exemption threshold defeats the rule and is a serious compliance failure
Your agency's own policy can be stricter than the Framework, and where it is, it binds you

chunks.heading: Recordkeeping obligations
chunks.summary: Keeping good records at every stage is a legal obligation under the State Records Act - and your defence if a decision is challenged.
chunks.text: Records are an essential part of an accountable and transparent government and all government employees are obligated to keep them. You must keep good records at every stage of a procurement to document your decisions and the reasons behind them. This is a legal obligation under the State Records Act and will help you answer any complaints or requests for public information. All information created, sent or received in the course of your work is a record; you do not own these records even when you create them yourself - the government does. Your purchasing records should show authorisation for the purchase, reasons for selection of the purchasing method, details of all offers obtained, supplier evaluation criteria and reasons for supplier selection, records of negotiations if applicable, completed purchase orders and payment documentation, evidence of receipt, acceptance and payment, and copies of all related correspondence. Keep emails and letters relating to business; RFx documents, purchase orders, contract documents, evidence of payment and receipts; notes of phone calls recording when the call occurred, who was involved, what was discussed, decisions made and advice given; meeting records with dates, times, locations, attendees, key discussion points and decisions; instant messages where they contain advice, decisions or approvals; text messages containing decisions or actions; and briefing notes, approvals, plans and reports. You do not need to keep sticky notes (make a proper record of the content instead), emails duplicating information already captured elsewhere, or unsolicited mail. If you are unsure whether to make or keep a record, ask: did I write, send, use or keep this in the course of my work; am I or is someone else required to act on this; will anyone need this information in the future?
checklist: Record the authorisation and the financial delegate who gave it
Record why you chose this purchasing method
Keep every offer received, not just the winning one
Record the evaluation criteria and the reasons for selecting the supplier
Record negotiations, including what was conceded and why
Keep the PO, invoices, evidence of receipt and evidence of payment
Make a file note of any substantive phone call or meeting with a supplier
watch_outs: Messages in chat apps count as records if they contain advice, decisions or approvals - get them into the system or repeat them in email
You cannot answer a GIPA request, a complaint or an audit from memory

chunks.heading: The three-stage best practice method: plan, source, manage
chunks.summary: Every procurement runs through plan, source and manage - each with three steps - plus disposal where relevant.
chunks.text: In the simplest terms, goods and services procurement involves planning to determine needs and define the right strategy, sourcing the right suppliers to provide goods or services, managing the rights and responsibilities of all parties involved, and disposing of goods when they are no longer required, where applicable. Procurement best practice follows three stages, each with three steps. Stage 1 Planning involves engaging with stakeholders to identify their needs, conducting market research and forming a procurement strategy. Stage 2 Sourcing includes approaching the market, evaluating offers, negotiating and awarding a contract. Stage 3 Managing is not the end of the process - signing a contract is the start of an ongoing relationship with the supplier to ensure you get what you contracted for, including monitoring supplier performance, reporting, ensuring the supplier is paid, and acting as a point of contact if issues arise.

chunks.heading: How much planning is enough
chunks.summary: Scale the planning effort to the size, value and complexity of the buy - but never skip it entirely.
chunks.text: Investing effort in planning directly contributes to better procurement outcomes. It helps ensure value for money, reduces risks and increases opportunities for sustainable procurement and innovation. Many procurements that have issues during the Manage stage arise because of poor planning. Even simple procurements require some basic planning prior to conducting the purchase. The effort you put into planning should be proportionate to the size, value and complexity of your procurement. Low value, simple purchases are less likely to need elaborate planning. However, a degree of effort is always required to understand the business need, analyse the supply market, consider your options, and plan the procurement.
watch_outs: Most contract management problems are planning problems that surfaced late

chunks.heading: Analyse the business need and engage stakeholders
chunks.summary: Separate what stakeholders want from what the business actually needs, and get their buy-in early.
chunks.text: Getting a good understanding of what is really needed is critical for ensuring that the goods or services you procure are fit for purpose and achieve value for money. Considering quantity, capability, cost, timing and quality helps you plan a procurement that will satisfy the business need. At the start of the project engage your stakeholders to understand their needs and win their commitment to your procurement strategy. Stakeholders are people or organisations with an interest in the procurement because it affects them or because you need their support. Identify whether they are internal or external, involve them early to help inform, improve and shape your planning, and understand any concerns they may have and how they could positively or negatively influence the procurement. Demand for goods or services can be initiated in several ways, verbal or written, from a variety of stakeholders, and it is common for stakeholders to produce a long list of things they want rather than what they need to address the problem. When defining the business need you should consider both current and future requirements, explore ideas and alternatives for delivering the same outcome, define the need so potential suppliers can clearly understand the requirement, and seek agreement from your stakeholders. When considering alternatives, think about challenging the demand (are the goods and services really needed), alternative methods of meeting the demand, reducing the frequency of use, reusing or recycling, simplifying or standardising specifications, and reducing the product and service range and complexity.
checklist: Map internal and external stakeholders and what each one needs from this procurement
Write the business need as a problem to be solved, not as a product to be bought
Challenge the demand: is this genuinely needed, at this frequency, at this specification?
Test alternatives - reuse, standardise, reduce range, reduce frequency
Get written agreement from stakeholders on the defined need before you go further
watch_outs: A wants list dressed up as a requirement produces an over-specified tender and a narrow field of bidders

chunks.heading: Analyse the supply market
chunks.summary: Five practical steps to understand prices, players, competitiveness and alternatives before you commit to an approach.
chunks.text: Market analysis is about understanding how the market for particular goods or services works. Without this information it can be difficult to decide on the best way to approach the market or to assess the risks associated with your procurement. Analysing the market helps you understand typical prices, the size of the market, who the key suppliers are and their location, how competitive the market is, alternative goods and services, market trends, new and innovative solutions, suppliers' capability and capacity to deliver, solutions implemented by other agencies, and your agency's buying power. There are five practical steps. Step 1: consider existing procurement arrangements - first check whether the goods or services are available on an existing arrangement. Step 2: identify suppliers using the buy.nsw Supplier Hub, including local businesses, SMEs, regional businesses, Aboriginal businesses and social enterprises. Registration is required to view supplier profiles and products. When suppliers join the Supplier Hub they can add business identifiers, which are either self-identified (shown blue) or verified through a third party (shown green) - for example a verified Aboriginal owned business, disability employment organisation, verified social enterprise or gender equitable employer. Step 3: gather information about goods and services by requesting information from suppliers, checking their websites and marketing materials, and arranging demonstrations; this is also a good opportunity to ask about their sustainable procurement methods. Step 4: research customer reviews, comparison sites and industry bodies or experts. Step 5: learn from others - check whether another agency has procured something similar and seek their advice and lessons learned.
checklist: Check existing whole-of-government, scheme and agency arrangements first
Search the Supplier Hub and note which identifiers are verified (green) versus self-declared (blue)
Gather product and service information directly from suppliers, including their sustainability practices
Look at independent reviews, comparison sites and industry bodies
Ask another agency or council that has bought something similar what they learned

chunks.heading: Building supplier due diligence into your plan
chunks.summary: Due diligence checks are mostly done at sourcing, but you design them at planning - and you write them into the market documents.
chunks.text: Supplier due diligence refers to the checks you perform on potential suppliers to understand whether they are genuine, are capable and reliable, are financially viable, have the required authorities, licences and status, and are of good repute and integrity. While most due diligence tasks are performed during the sourcing stage after potential suppliers have been identified, it is important to consider due diligence when planning your procurement. This includes identifying the capabilities that will be required to fulfil the procurement, understanding the regulatory environment that applies to suppliers in the market, and deciding how to approach the market, what information suppliers will need to provide, and how that information will be verified. You should include due diligence measures in your procurement strategy and in your market-facing documents. The ICAC Supplier Due Diligence guide sets out specific checks you can make.
checklist: List the capabilities, licences and insurances the work genuinely requires
Identify the regulatory regime that applies to suppliers in this market
Decide what evidence suppliers must supply, and how you will verify it independently
Write those requirements into the RFx documents, not just into your internal plan

chunks.heading: Finalise and approve your procurement strategy
chunks.summary: The strategy answers ten questions and must be approved by the right delegate before you go anywhere near the market.
chunks.text: To be successful you should develop a strategy that considers your business needs, the market, risks and opportunities. Obtaining approval for the expenditure is critically important. For low value, low risk procurements and simple purchases, a briefing note or email approval may be used as the procurement strategy - check with your agency's procurement team. When developing your strategy consider: what is needed and why, what the benefits are, and whether it will deliver environmental, social or economic outcomes; the total estimated contract value; what the supply market looks like; whether there are existing contracts or schemes you should use; whether your procurement should preference certain types of suppliers, and whether it qualifies for exemptions; the risks you face and how you will manage them; the type of market approach you will use and why; what success will look like; and timings, including when existing arrangements conclude and when you need to release market documents. To finalise the strategy: summarise your key findings on business needs, market analysis, and risks and opportunities; include the total estimated contract value and contract period including any extensions, and your strategy for approaching the market; identify the benefits of the procurement outcome; make sure you have enough support from stakeholders; and get approval from your manager, director or agency head as per your agency's financial delegations.
checklist: State the need, the benefits, and any environmental, social or economic outcomes
State the total estimated contract value including all extension options
Summarise the market analysis and what it tells you about the right approach
Confirm whether an existing contract or scheme must be used
Identify any supplier preferencing obligations and any exemptions you are relying on
Set out the risks and how each will be managed
Define what success looks like and how it will be measured
Map the timeline back from when the current arrangement ends
Get written approval from the correct financial delegate before approaching the market
watch_outs: Approaching the market before the strategy is approved is one of the most common compliance failures
Understating the contract value by leaving out extension options can put you on the wrong side of a threshold

chunks.heading: Get authorised to approach the market
chunks.summary: Four things must be in place before you can go to market: accreditation, an approved strategy, process arrangements and budget approval.
chunks.text: The way you approach and engage with suppliers is often referred to as going to market or a market approach. There is no one-size-fits-all approach; choose one that best fits your situation based on the value, complexity, timing and goals of your procurement. Generally, the higher the value or risk, the more rigorous the market approach, and simple purchases are less likely to require a formal market approach. You must be authorised to approach the market. To be authorised you need the appropriate level of agency accreditation, an approved procurement strategy, arrangements in place to manage all stages of the procurement process and outcome, and adequate budget and approval from your financial delegate. The contract value helps determine whether you are accredited to conduct the procurement and whether your agency head or another delegate can approve the procurement and sign the contract. Remember to consider local suppliers, social enterprises, disability employment organisations, SMEs, regional, gender equitable and Aboriginal businesses as per exemptions and preferences. You also have environmental considerations so you can meet mandatory requirements, improve value for money and achieve sustainability benefits. If you estimate your procurement is over $680,000 you must apply the Enforceable Procurement Provisions Board Direction. If your procurement is over $7.5 million you are required to embed upfront local market testing in your procurement plan as per PBD-2024-02.
checklist: Confirm your agency's accreditation covers this value and risk level
Confirm the procurement strategy is approved, in writing
Confirm you have the people and process in place to run all stages, including contract management
Confirm budget and financial delegate approval
Check the EPP threshold ($680,000 ex GST for goods and services)
Check the $7.5 million local market testing requirement
Check supplier preferencing obligations before you design the approach

chunks.heading: Choosing your market approach: RFI, EOI, RFQ, RFP, RFT
chunks.summary: Five common approaches, and when each one is the right tool.
chunks.text: Request for Information (RFI): a useful way to better understand the market before starting a procurement. You invite suppliers to provide information about their capabilities, solutions and emerging trends without committing to purchase. This helps you test assumptions, refine requirements and identify what the market can offer. Most effective for higher risk or more complex procurements, or where requirements are not yet fully defined, and often used early in the lifecycle to inform your strategy. Expression of Interest (EOI): use where you are uncertain about the goods or services you are procuring. It helps you find out what is available and whether suppliers are interested and capable. You do not include price information or award a contract; instead you usually shortlist potential suppliers and invite them to tender. Benefits include testing whether a good or service exists, keeping costs down by only inviting capable suppliers to respond, and encouraging competition. Request for Quote (RFQ): a simple and efficient way to procure goods and services you understand well and use frequently. You invite potential suppliers to provide a quote for specific goods or services, often from a list of registered suppliers on a prequalification scheme. Most effective for low risk, low-to-medium-value procurements with well-defined requirements and standard terms and conditions. Request for Proposal (RFP): helps you explore solutions and draw out a detailed response to a specific problem or need, and can tap into new and innovative approaches. Like an EOI it is often the first step in a multi-stage process; once you have proposals you can shortlist suppliers and invite them to tender or negotiate directly with your preferred supplier. Include criteria to evaluate suppliers' expertise, experience and capacity to deliver. Open Request for Tender (RFT): works best when there is a broad and competitive market, that market is dynamic and subject to change, your procurement is high value, and there is likely to be a lot of supplier interest. Anybody can submit a tender and tenderers must show they satisfy the evaluation criteria. An open RFT encourages competition and is effective for ensuring value for money, making it attractive when you are unsure of pricing or do not know who can supply what you need. Multi-stage or selective RFT: works best when you want to establish a panel of suppliers for ongoing work, identify several potential suppliers for a single contract, or identify the supplier with the best solution to a complex or unusual procurement. It reduces tendering costs for both sides and helps quickly identify the best suppliers in a mature marketplace. It usually involves two stages: identify suitable prospective suppliers, for example from a prequalification scheme or via an EOI, then shortlist applicants who have demonstrated they can fulfil the criteria and invite the best to tender.
keywords: best way to go to market
checklist: Do you know exactly what you need? If not, start with an RFI or EOI
Is it well defined, low risk and low-to-medium value? An RFQ off a scheme is usually right
Do you want the market to propose solutions? Use an RFP
Is it high value with a broad competitive market? Use an open RFT
Do you need a panel or a shortlist first? Use a multi-stage RFT

chunks.heading: Your evaluation plan
chunks.summary: The evaluation plan must be finalised before the tender closes and before any response is opened.
chunks.text: Your evaluation plan should include details of your evaluation team members and their responsibilities; evaluation protocols covering the evaluation process, managing confidentiality and conflicts of interest, record keeping, communicating with respondents, and negotiation protocols; clearly defined evaluation criteria and weightings; and how the successful supplier should be recommended for contract award and notification. You must finalise your evaluation plan before the tender period closes and before opening supplier responses.
keywords: what templates for a tender evaluation
watch_outs: Writing or changing the evaluation plan after responses are opened is a serious probity breach

chunks.heading: Setting evaluation criteria and weightings
chunks.summary: Mandatory criteria are pass/fail and must be real needs; non-mandatory criteria are weighted across price and non-price.
chunks.text: Your evaluation plan and tender documents should include the mandatory and non-mandatory criteria you will use to evaluate supplier responses and select the successful supplier. Mandatory criteria should reflect actual needs and not wants; suppliers must meet them to be considered further. Non-mandatory criteria are what your evaluation team will use to evaluate responses to a competitive market approach, and these can be weighted to give more importance to some criteria. Your criteria are made up of price and non-price criteria and you should determine the importance of each by applying a percentage; for example price might have a weighting of 60 per cent and the non-price criteria 40 per cent. Examples of non-price criteria include quality and quantity, fitness for purpose, technical requirements, ability to meet quality or performance standards, the supplier's experience and performance history, and environmental sustainability. Your criteria could also address government priorities such as supporting SMEs and regional businesses, providing employment and business opportunities for Aboriginal people, and supporting apprenticeships and trainees. The SME and Regional Procurement Policy includes mandatory minimum non-price evaluation criteria for contracts over $3 million; you can apply these criteria below this value as a way of supporting SME participation and NSW Government's economic, ethical, environmental and social priorities. Your RFx documents should include key evaluation criteria and their relative importance, although you should not publish individual weightings.
checklist: Test every mandatory criterion: is this a genuine need, or a want that will exclude good suppliers?
Set price and non-price weightings before you see any response
Check whether the $3 million SME mandatory minimum non-price criteria apply
Publish the criteria and their relative importance, but not the individual weightings
Make sure the criteria can actually be scored from the information you asked suppliers to provide

chunks.heading: Forming the evaluation team and declaring conflicts
chunks.summary: The team combines business users and technical experts, and every member declares conflicts before the approach opens.
chunks.text: Your evaluation team should include business users and technical experts who will evaluate supplier responses and form a recommendation. Their role includes reviewing and assessing each response in accordance with the evaluation criteria and methodology in your evaluation plan, making clarifications with respondents, undertaking reference checks if required, summarising the assessment results and recommending the successful respondents, identifying areas for negotiation, and signing off the final evaluation report including the recommendation. Before approaching the market you should develop and implement a conduct plan to ensure your evaluation team works within a framework of probity and fair dealing. This includes declaring any conflicts of interest.
checklist: Include both business users and technical experts
Issue and sign the procurement conduct plan before the approach opens
Collect a conflict of interest declaration from every team member, including observers and advisers
Re-check for conflicts when the respondent list is known - a conflict can appear at that point
Have the whole team sign off the final evaluation report

chunks.heading: Preparing your RFx documents
chunks.summary: Eight things your market documents must tell suppliers, plus a response template so offers are comparable.
chunks.text: Before you can approach the market you need to prepare your RFx documents. To get a successful outcome you need to provide suppliers with all the information they need to submit the best fit for purpose bid. You must provide the same level of information and equal treatment to all prospective suppliers. You will also need to provide suppliers with a response template, which helps ensure responses are provided in a consistent way that can be reasonably compared and evaluated. Your RFx documents should include a description of the goods or services you are procuring; the contract duration or the period the goods or services must be provided (generally you should not make the contract last longer than 5 years including any extensions); where and how suppliers can lodge their responses; the due date for responses; any conditions suppliers must meet to be considered for the contract; key evaluation criteria and their relative importance, although you should not provide individual weightings; whether the procurement process contains any further steps; and your contact details and how prospective suppliers can ask for further information.
checklist: Describe what you are buying in outcome terms a supplier outside your organisation can understand
State the contract term and every extension option
State exactly where and how to lodge, and the closing date and time
State the conditions of participation and the mandatory criteria
State the evaluation criteria and their relative importance
Say whether there are further stages after this one
Give a named contact and a channel for questions
Attach a response template so offers arrive comparable

chunks.heading: Issuing your RFx and setting the tender period
chunks.summary: Use Supplier Hub and eTendering; allow 25 days as a default, 10 in defined circumstances, and avoid closing on weekends or public holidays.
chunks.text: There are two whole-of-government systems you can use to find suppliers and approach the market, and your agency may also have its own. The Supplier Hub is where you find suppliers ready to sell to government. NSW eTendering is where you request quotes from suppliers on prequalification schemes, advertise and manage tenders, list upcoming or closed business opportunities, and list awarded contracts valued over $150,000 (inc GST). When determining your tender period, consider your needs and the suppliers' ability to prepare a proper response. Allow a minimum of 25 calendar days if you publish the tender on NSW eTendering. Ten calendar days is the minimum recommended if information about the procurement has been published in your agency's annual procurement plan within the last 12 months, for buying goods or services using approved procurement arrangements such as prequalification schemes, and for recurring procurement arrangements. There are no set minimum tender periods for urgent procurements such as responding to a critical issue or an emergency. Your agency may have specific timeframe requirements based on value, risk and complexity. If your procurement is for goods and services valued over $680,000 (ex GST) it may be subject to the enforceable procurement provisions, including the minimum tender periods for covered procurements. Try to avoid closing your tender on public holidays or weekends; the system sets a standard closing time of 3pm for all opportunities. Suppliers are often preparing their response right up until the closing date and time and may need to contact you if there are issues submitting. You must give suppliers as much notice as possible of upcoming procurements.

chunks.heading: Running the process: questions, addenda, mistakes, late tenders and extensions
chunks.summary: Five rules for keeping a live market approach fair and defensible.
chunks.text: Step 1, respond to questions and clarifications. You must reply promptly to any questions or requests for clarification from respondents. Your answers should be deidentified and supplied to all respondents, and the information you provide must not give one supplier an advantage over another. Step 2, issuing addenda or amendments. If you issue an addendum you must give suppliers reasonable time to modify and re-submit their response, and make reasonable efforts to notify all prospective respondents, for example by emailing all suppliers that downloaded the tender documents. Generally you should not issue an addendum within 5 working days of a tender closing date; if this is not possible you should consider extending the tender period by at least 5 working days. Step 3, allowing suppliers to correct mistakes. If you let a supplier correct an unintentional error during the tender period you must give all suppliers the same opportunity. Step 4, late tender submissions. You should not accept a late tender submission unless your action or omission caused the lateness, or you are sure no other bidder will be disadvantaged. Your tender documents should clearly state whether you will accept late submissions and in what circumstances. Step 5, extending the tender period. You should not extend the tender period except in exceptional circumstances, for example where you need to issue late addenda; a request from one or more suppliers for an extension is not an exceptional circumstance. Throughout, you must provide the same level of information and equal treatment to all prospective suppliers, always use secure processes to manage responses, and maintain the confidentiality of all supplier proposals.
checklist: Deidentify every question and circulate the answer to all respondents
Do not issue an addendum inside 5 working days of close without extending the period
Notify everyone who downloaded the documents when you issue an addendum
If you let one supplier fix an error, offer the same to all
Only accept a late tender if you caused the lateness or no bidder is disadvantaged - and say so in the documents up front
watch_outs: Answering one supplier's question privately is one of the fastest ways to compromise a process
A supplier asking for more time is not, by itself, an exceptional circumstance

chunks.heading: Evaluating responses and selecting a supplier
chunks.summary: Three steps: rule out non-conforming responses, score the rest against your criteria, then document the recommendation.
chunks.text: After the tender closes, open the responses and have the evaluation team evaluate them and recommend the successful supplier. To select the successful supplier the evaluation team must follow the processes documented in your evaluation plan and procurement conduct plan. Step 1: rule out responses that do not meet the tender conditions and mandatory criteria. Step 2: assess the remaining responses against your non-mandatory evaluation criteria; you can use the buy.nsw evaluation scoresheet, which includes guidance on scoring how well a supplier's response meets your requirements. Step 3: recommend the successful supplier, documenting the evaluation team's recommendations in an evaluation report. You must use a framework of probity and fair dealing to select the suppliers you assess are most likely to deliver value for money.

chunks.heading: Supplier due diligence before you engage
chunks.summary: Before finalising an engagement, verify the supplier is real, capable, solvent, licensed and reputable - it is your responsibility.
chunks.text: Supplier due diligence refers to the checks you perform on potential suppliers to understand whether they are genuine, are capable and reliable, are financially viable, have the required authorities, licences and status, and are of good repute and integrity. This helps you ensure value for money, prevent corrupt conduct, maintain trust in public administration, and comply with legal and regulatory expectations. Ensuring that suppliers are legitimate and capable of delivering the specified goods or services is your responsibility. After identifying potential suppliers, and before finalising the engagement, you must verify that suppliers are capable of performing the work and have provided truthful information about their skills, experience, business records and qualifications. This applies both to individual procurement activities and when creating a panel of prequalified suppliers.

chunks.heading: Negotiate and award the contract
chunks.summary: Use an existing contract template where one exists; get legal advice before you modify one. Purchase orders are contracts too.
chunks.text: A contract is an agreement made between two or more parties where legal rights and obligations are created that are enforceable in law. Your contracts should always be commercial and make it easy for suppliers to understand their obligations and your needs. Generally you should not make the contract last longer than 5 years, including any extensions. For more complex procurements you may need to negotiate to achieve the best possible arrangement with your preferred suppliers; good negotiation leaves both parties satisfied. When you award a contract, use an existing contract template where one exists, because they include standard terms and conditions. If there is no template, or you need to modify an existing template, you may need to negotiate new contract terms with the supplier, and you should seek legal advice if you do. Refer to buy.nsw for information on contract clauses and requirements including insurances, indemnity, intellectual property, reporting and termination. You should use model tender and contract clauses for goods and services contracts over $7.5 million to meet the requirements of the Small Business Shorter Payment Terms Policy. When you procure certain types of goods or services, such as those from prequalification schemes, you must use existing contract templates - this includes procuring ICT and professional services. Purchase orders form the contract where you do not use a standalone contract, for example for low value purchases where no contract template exists, when buying off a scheme where you do not issue a contract, and when buying off a standing offer or panel where no customer contract is issued. A purchase order is a commercial document issued by a buyer to a seller and is a legally binding contract once accepted; it indicates the types, quantities and agreed prices for goods or services and outlines the delivery date and payment terms, and is usually based on a quote provided by the seller. No contract exists until the purchase order is accepted by the seller.

chunks.heading: Debriefing unsuccessful suppliers
chunks.summary: A debrief is feedback to help the supplier improve, not a re-argument of the decision. SMEs and regional suppliers can require one.
chunks.text: After awarding a contract you should debrief unsuccessful suppliers. This is an opportunity to provide feedback on their response to help improve their future tender responses, not a debate on the evaluation process. You can conduct debriefings by telephone or in a face-to-face meeting. Your feedback should include strengths in the supplier's response and areas for improvement for future tender submissions.
