You must provide pre and post-tender briefings when reasonably requested by SMEs and regional suppliers, to clarify requirements and provide feedback on unsuccessful bids. You must not discuss commercial-in-confidence information, such as details of other suppliers' responses, and you must keep a record of the debrief including attendees.
checklist: Offer a debrief to every unsuccessful respondent
Prepare strengths and improvement areas from the evaluation record, not from memory
Do not disclose other suppliers' pricing, scores or content
Keep a written record of the debrief and who attended
If an SME or regional supplier reasonably requests a briefing, you must provide it
watch_outs: A debrief that turns into a defence of the decision usually generates a complaint rather than preventing one

chunks.heading: The manage stage starts at signature
chunks.summary: Signing is the start, not the end. Set up systems, allocate responsibilities, brief stakeholders and keep checking the supplier.
chunks.text: Signing a contract is not the end of the procurement process. It is the start of your ongoing relationship with the supplier, and you need to manage the contract to make sure the supplier delivers what they have committed to. Every arrangement sets out the rights and responsibilities of the parties, so it is important to identify, understand and manage them to better ensure you get what you contracted for. Key activities in this stage include paying suppliers in line with policies and procedures, including the Faster Payment Terms Policy and Small Business Shorter Payment Terms Policy; working with the supplier to establish systems and processes and determine who is responsible for key tasks and activities; engaging key stakeholders and communicating the details of the new arrangement to them; and conducting additional supplier due diligence checks.
checklist: Agree with the supplier who is responsible for each task and activity
Set up the systems and processes needed to run the contract before day one
Brief internal stakeholders on what the new arrangement means for them
Diarise the post-engagement due diligence checks
Confirm the payment path and the invoice requirements so payment clocks run correctly

chunks.heading: Paying suppliers on time
chunks.summary: Small business invoices between $10,000 and $1 million: 5 business days. Under $10,000: as fast as possible, ideally by PCard.
chunks.text: You must pay suppliers on time, especially small businesses. The Office of the Small Business Commissioner monitors and reports on agency payment performance to small businesses. You must pay correctly rendered invoices between $10,000 and $1 million from registered small businesses, those with fewer than 20 full-time equivalent employees, within 5 business days as per the Faster Payment Terms Policy. You should pay any correctly rendered invoice under $10,000 as soon as possible using a purchasing card or electronic funds transfer; check your agency's thresholds for PCard use. Large businesses with NSW Government goods and services contracts over $7.5 million must pay the small businesses they directly subcontract to within 20 business days upon receipt of a correctly rendered invoice, as per the Small Business Shorter Payment Terms Policy. If you are buying above your agency's PCard threshold you will generally need to request a purchase order using your agency's systems and processes. Purchase orders are commercial documents commonly used for low value, low risk procurements, and are often issued through ERP systems such as SAP and Oracle. Your PO should include details of the successful supplier's response or negotiated contract, or be based on a quote, and should include details of goods or services being purchased, quantities, agreed prices, delivery date and location, and payment terms. The supplier should include the PO number on their invoices to assist with faster payment processing. A purchasing card is a type of credit card; because there is a cost associated with raising and processing POs, agencies typically use PCards for low value purchases, which is better value for money, removes the need to raise a PO and automatically generates payment. When you use a PCard instead of a PO, the terms and conditions of the agreement are usually those of the seller rather than the buyer, so check you are able to comply.
checklist: Confirm whether the supplier is a registered small business - it changes the payment deadline
Check the invoice is correctly rendered before starting the clock, and tell the supplier promptly if it is not
Make sure the PO number is on the invoice
For contracts over $7.5 million, check the head contractor is paying its small business subcontractors within 20 business days
If paying by PCard, check you can comply with the seller's terms and conditions

citations.label: Small Business Shorter Payment Terms Policy
What is a correctly rendered invoice

chunks.heading: Reporting and contract disclosure obligations
chunks.summary: Contracts of $150,000 (inc GST) or more must be publicly disclosed within 45 working days and stay listed for at least 20 days.
chunks.text: You have several reporting and disclosure obligations once a procurement contract is active. Under the GIPA Act 2009 you must disclose all contracts over $150,000 (inc GST) within 45 working days of the contract coming into effect. Agencies do this by publicly publishing the contract details on NSW eTendering and ensuring the entry remains listed for at least 20 days or until the contract is complete, whichever is longer. Your agency must also report on its record of on-time paying in its annual report. Councils have an equivalent obligation: under section 27 of the GIPA Act a council must maintain a public contracts register recording information about each contract with a private sector body valued at $150,000 (inc GST) or more, published within 45 days of the contract becoming effective and kept available for 20 working days or until the obligations under the contract have been satisfied, whichever is longer. Contracts are classified as Class 1 (value of $150,000 or more), Class 2 (Class 1 contracts requiring additional information in certain circumstances) and Class 3 (Class 2 contracts valued at $5 million or more). Agencies and councils are not required to publish certain confidential information, including commercial-in-confidence provisions and information where there is an overriding public interest against disclosure.
checklist: Diarise the 45-day disclosure deadline from the date the contract takes effect
Classify the contract (Class 1, 2 or 3) and publish the right level of detail
Identify genuinely commercial-in-confidence content before publishing - and only that
Keep the entry live for at least 20 days, or until the contract completes if that is longer

citations.label: IPC NSW - Register of government contracts

chunks.heading: Managing supplier performance and the relationship
chunks.summary: Regardless of value, you must actively manage the arrangement: performance against KPIs, regular contact, and policy reporting from the supplier.
chunks.text: Regardless of the value of your arrangement you need to manage it. It is important to communicate regularly and foster a positive relationship with your supplier to ensure the original objective is met and value for money is achieved. This includes expediting or following up on an order; managing supplier performance and relationships to ensure delivery of commitments; reviewing how the contract is performing against agreed key performance indicators; conducting post-engagement due diligence checks, especially for lengthy contracts; and ensuring suppliers meet reporting requirements, including those in the Aboriginal Procurement Policy, the SME and Regional Procurement Policy, and the Small Business Shorter Payment Terms Policy. Regular contact will help you identify and address any problems early.
checklist: Confirm the KPIs in the contract are measurable and that you actually receive the data to measure them
Set a regular contract meeting rhythm and hold it even when things are going well
Track policy reporting the supplier owes you under the APP, SME and Regional, and Shorter Payment Terms policies
Re-run due diligence periodically on long contracts
Escalate small performance issues early, in writing, before they become disputes
watch_outs: A KPI nobody reports on is not a KPI - check the reporting mechanism exists from day one

chunks.heading: Running contract management meetings and reviewing schedules
chunks.summary: A practical operating rhythm for a live service contract: agenda, evidence, schedule reviews, variations and escalation.
chunks.text: For an ongoing service contract, contract management usually settles into a routine built around scheduled meetings, performance reporting and periodic schedule reviews. A workable operating rhythm looks like this. Before the meeting, collect the supplier's performance report against the contract KPIs, your own service data and any complaints or incidents logged since the last meeting, and circulate an agenda in advance. Run the meeting to a standing agenda: actions from last time, safety and incidents, performance against each KPI with the evidence behind it, complaints and service failures, financial matters including invoices, variations and any abatements, upcoming works or changes, and risks. Record decisions and actions with owners and due dates, and issue the minutes - these are records under the State Records Act and they are the evidence base if performance later has to be enforced. Reviewing contract schedules means checking that the operational annexures still match reality: the service specification, the price or rate schedule and any indexation mechanism, the KPI and reporting schedule, the asset or equipment list, and the service area or route definitions. Where reality has drifted from the schedule, deal with it as a formal variation with a documented value-for-money and delegation assessment - do not let it settle in as an informal practice. Where performance falls short, use the remedies the contract actually gives you, in order: informal escalation, a written performance notice, a rectification or improvement plan with a deadline, then the contractual abatement, step-in or termination rights. Keep the paper trail complete at every step, because remedies that were never formally invoked are very hard to rely on later.
checklist: Circulate an agenda and the performance pack before each contract meeting
Work through KPIs one by one against evidence, not against impressions
Record decisions, actions, owners and due dates - and file the minutes as a record
Review the service specification, rate schedule and indexation, KPI schedule, asset list and service areas at set intervals
Handle any drift from the schedules as a formal variation with a documented value for money and delegation assessment
Escalate performance failures through the contract's own remedies, in writing, in order
watch_outs: Informal scope creep agreed in a meeting and never varied is a common audit finding and can leave the contract unenforceable in that area
Approving a variation without checking the delegation and the value for money case repeats the original procurement decision without the original rigour

chunks.heading: Receiving and accepting goods
chunks.summary: Delivery is not acceptance. Check against the contract before you accept, because acceptance discharges the supplier's obligation.
chunks.text: When receiving goods you need to check they meet the requirements of the contract. This is called acceptance and includes checking the goods against delivery dockets and descriptions on the quote or purchase order; inspecting for damage; rejecting damaged goods and returning them; accepting conforming goods and signing the carrier's delivery docket as a receipt; and informing accounts payable that you have received the goods. Most purchase order terms and conditions do not regard delivery of goods as acceptance. Acceptance refers to the agency checking to ensure that the supplies meet the requirements of the contract. If the goods meet the requirements of the purchase order, the supplier has fulfilled their contractual obligations.
watch_outs: Signing for delivery is not the same as accepting the goods - check against the PO first

chunks.heading: Post-engagement due diligence
chunks.summary: Re-check insurances, licences and financial health on long contracts - and always re-verify a change of bank account details.
chunks.text: Some due diligence checks may need to be repeated after engaging a supplier, particularly for lengthy contracts. This may be as simple as checking that the supplier's insurances and licences remain current. For more complex contracts it may require ongoing checks on the supplier's structure, financial health and regulatory compliance. Additional due diligence is also required if the supplier requests a change to its bank account details.
checklist: Diarise insurance and licence expiry dates and chase renewals before they lapse
Re-check the supplier's corporate structure and financial health periodically on long contracts
Treat any request to change bank details as a fraud risk: verify independently, using contact details you already hold, never those in the request
watch_outs: Payment redirection fraud usually arrives as a routine-looking request to update bank details - always verify through a channel you established earlier

chunks.heading: Renewing the arrangement
chunks.summary: Start the next procurement before this one ends: review what worked, then re-analyse demand and market.
chunks.text: Part of the manage stage is considering your strategy for the next arrangement and planning for renewal. You should be continually assessing and improving your procurement strategy and processes to help provide the best possible outcome for the next arrangement. Before the contract expires, review the strengths and weaknesses of the existing contract with the supplier and internal stakeholders, and analyse the demand and the market to inform your next procurement strategy.
checklist: Work back from the contract end date - a full retender needs planning, approval and a tender period
Run a joint review with the supplier and with internal stakeholders on what worked and what did not
Re-analyse demand: has the need changed since the last time?
Re-analyse the market: are there new suppliers, technologies or arrangements?
Decide whether to extend, retender or go a different way, and get that decision approved
watch_outs: Leaving the retender too late usually forces either an unplanned extension or a rushed process - both weaken value for money

chunks.heading: What probity means
chunks.summary: Probity is more than avoiding corruption - it is acting ethically, with integrity, uprightness and honesty.
chunks.text: Probity is more than simply avoiding corrupt or dishonest conduct. Probity means acting ethically, with integrity, uprightness and honesty. For public officials and public sector agencies, creating and maintaining probity involves applying and complying with public sector values and probity principles such as impartiality, accountability and transparency. Procurement is an area that is vulnerable to corruption and maladministration, and you are obligated to ensure your procurement conduct is probity rich. Not upholding probity principles can damage your agency's reputation, diminish the government's standing as a business partner, lead to poor procurement outcomes, and lead to disciplinary action.

chunks.heading: The four probity principles
chunks.summary: Value for money, impartiality, consistency and fairness, and accountability and transparency.
chunks.text: As a public official you have a duty to adopt processes, practices and behaviour that enhance and promote honesty and integrity and protect the public interest. Your conduct must always be fair, ethical, transparent and accountable. Corrupt conduct violates key probity principles and can occur at any point in the procurement process, so upholding these principles helps prevent corruption. Suppliers often invest significant time, effort and resources in preparing and submitting offers, and in return are entitled to expect fair treatment at every stage. Principle 1, value for money: obtaining value for money is a fundamental principle of any procurement. Corrupted procurements do not deliver best value for money. Ensure the goods and services you procure are fit for purpose, that you understand the whole-of-life costs, and that they are appropriate. Good supplier due diligence helps because it increases the probability of engaging a high-performing, reliable supplier. Principle 2, impartiality: since we are spending public money it must be spent in an unbiased way. If you fail to act with impartiality, or even just appear to be biased, suppliers and the public may consider the process unfair, which can result in actual corrupt conduct, suppliers approaching officials seeking favourable treatment, reputational damage, suppliers being deterred from doing business with government, and suppliers taking legal action resulting in delays and significant costs. Principle 3, consistency and fairness: a clear, visible and meaningful commitment to fairness creates a level playing field and supports competition. Being fair and equitable means giving all suppliers the same access to information, guidance and instructions. Consistently applied processes help prevent discrimination and remove opportunities for corruption. Principle 4, accountability and transparency: taking responsibility for your decisions and ensuring decision-making processes are clear and open gives the public confidence and reduces opportunities for fraud and corruption to go undiscovered. All procurement decisions must be able to stand up to public scrutiny - always ask yourself whether you can explain and defend your decisions if they come under scrutiny. Good record keeping is key. The integrity of competitive procurement also hinges on maintaining appropriate confidentiality to protect information provided by suppliers, and information security makes it harder for a supplier to gain an unfair advantage. Public sector procurement can also help prevent unethical practices in the supply chain: due diligence checks can ensure suppliers and subcontractors pay fair wages, avoid child labour and source materials ethically.
checklist: Can you explain and defend this decision if it were made public tomorrow?
Has every supplier had the same access to the same information at the same time?
Is there anything in your process that a reasonable person could read as favouritism?
Is supplier confidential information secured and access-controlled?
Is the record complete enough for someone else to reconstruct why you decided as you did?

chunks.heading: Probity advisers and auditors
chunks.summary: Engaging a probity adviser does not transfer accountability, and should be the exception rather than the rule.
chunks.text: Probity advisers and auditors monitor or verify that your procurement processes are consistent with government regulations and probity principles. Engaging a probity adviser is not a way to outsource accountability for probity, and it is not a substitute for good management practices; it does not guarantee there will be no probity or process breaches. You and your agency are always accountable. Using external probity advisers and auditors should be the exception rather than the rule, as per the Procurement Policy Framework. You may need to engage a probity adviser or auditor if the integrity of the process, or part of it, may be questioned; if the project is politically sensitive or potentially controversial; when establishing or renewing contracts for goods or services that are vulnerable to being influenced by corrupt practices; to avoid a perception of bias or favouritism; where the process is extremely complex; or where there are substantial costs involved in preparing submissions or substantial government funding involved.
watch_outs: A probity adviser's sign-off is not a defence if the underlying decision was poor - accountability stays with you and your agency

chunks.heading: What counts as corrupt conduct
chunks.summary: Corrupt conduct is deliberate wrongdoing involving a NSW public official - not negligence or a mistake.
chunks.text: Corrupt conduct is deliberate or intentional wrongdoing, not negligence or a mistake. It has to involve or affect a New South Wales public official or public sector organisation. Corrupt conduct occurs when a public official improperly uses, or tries to improperly use, the knowledge, power or resources of their position for personal gain or the advantage of others; or dishonestly or improperly exercises their official functions in a partial manner or in a way that breaches public trust; or misuses information or material acquired during the course of their official functions. It also occurs when a member of the public influences, or tries to influence, a public official to use their position in a way that is dishonest or partial. And it occurs when the actions of any person impair, or could impair, public confidence in public administration - this could involve collusive tendering, fraud in relation to applications for licences or permits, dishonestly obtaining or benefiting from public funds or assets for private advantage, defrauding the public revenue, or fraudulently obtaining or retaining a position as a public official. Conduct is only corrupt if it could constitute or involve a criminal offence, a disciplinary offence, reasonable grounds for dismissal, or a substantial breach of an applicable code of conduct for Ministers and MPs. Examples in procurement include a public official providing confidential information to a supplier to give them an unfair advantage; an official secretly owning a private company, submitting bids and influencing the assessment; an official colluding with a contractor to falsify or inflate invoices; deliberately over-ordering goods and keeping the extra for private use; and two suppliers colluding to artificially elevate prices or manipulate which of them wins the work.

chunks.heading: The four unwanted outcomes that signal corruption
chunks.summary: Overcharging, underdelivery, overservicing and incorrect supplier choice - manage these and you detect corruption earlier.
chunks.text: Corruption in procurement can be difficult to detect because it often involves a secret arrangement that two or more corrupt parties are happy with. However, you can better detect and prevent corruption if you understand and manage unwanted procurement outcomes. These outcomes could be due to poor systems and practices, but they can also result from corrupt conduct. Overcharging: corruption usually involves the improper transfer of something valuable from public to private hands, and one of the most direct ways is intentional overcharging - approving unnecessary or over-priced contract variations, accepting unreasonably high bids and paying an excessive price, and paying invoices improperly charged above contract rates. Underdelivery: receiving less than what was expected and paid for - paying invoices where no items are delivered, receiving lesser quality goods or services than specified such as less thorough advice or poorer service, and receiving a lesser quantity than specified such as fewer computers or less regular cleaning. Overservicing: ordering and paying for items surplus to agency needs or of a higher quality or specification than required, even if the correct price is paid. Incorrect supplier choice: a supplier being awarded work undeservedly, including through confidential information being leaked to give them an advantage, assessment criteria weighted to favour a bid, and suppliers lying about their capability or credentials. The impacts of corrupt conduct include direct financial loss, wasted resources, reduced operational effectiveness, lowered staff morale, reputational damage to the agency and individual staff, and erosion of public trust.
checklist: Spot-check invoices against contract rates rather than assuming they are correct
Verify that what was ordered was actually delivered, in the quantity and quality specified
Question variations - particularly recurring ones on the same contract
Question specifications that are richer than the business need requires
Test claimed capability and credentials rather than accepting them on the response form

chunks.heading: Conflicts of interest
chunks.summary: A conflict exists when a reasonable person might perceive personal interests could be favoured over public duty. Conflicts are not wrong - failing to manage them is.
chunks.text: Conflicts of interest can lead to corrupt conduct, and even honest public officials may be unintentionally biased by their relationships and interests. A conflict of interest exists when a reasonable person might perceive that a public official's personal interests could be favoured over their public duties. Personal interests include family and friends, career opportunities, financial interests, and power and influence. Public duty includes performing your duties, complying with policies and procedures, and serving the public interest, your agency and the public in an ethical manner. Personal interests that may trigger a conflict include: pecuniary interests, involving actual or potential financial gain or loss, such as sources of income including secondary employment, ownership or lease of land, buildings and property, shares or investments, or an option to buy or sell an asset. People who are more than acquaintances - spouses, relatives including by marriage and close family friends, friends, current romantic partners, close colleagues and mentors, and social connections; feelings of animosity towards a person can also constitute a personal interest. People providing income - providers of secondary or other employment, current or former business partners, customers, significant suppliers or contractors of a private business or secondary employer, future employment or business opportunities for you or a family member, and relationships with former employers and colleagues especially where there is ongoing social contact. Organisations and clubs and people connected to them, including professional, sporting, recreational, community, arts or social organisations. People and entities who give benefits or favours, where you could feel or be perceived to feel indebted - gifts, benefits or hospitality more than token in nature, favours or valuable advice, discounts on goods and services, borrowing equipment, and sponsorships or donations to causes associated with you. Close connections including social media associations; you should be prudent about how you use social media and generally avoid endorsing products, services or companies connected to your work. Four elements determine whether a conflict exists: does the official have a personal interest; does the official have a public duty; is there a connection between the personal interest and the public duty; and could a reasonable person perceive that the personal interest might be favoured? Conflicts of interest are not wrong in themselves - it is how you manage them that matters. To protect yourself and your agency you must disclose all conflicts of interest and follow your agency's conflicts of interest management policy.
checklist: Apply the four-element test: personal interest, public duty, connection, reasonable person perception
Declare actual, potential and perceived conflicts - all three
Declare again when the respondent list becomes known
Follow your agency or council's conflicts of interest management policy for the treatment, not just the declaration
Record the declaration and the management strategy in the procurement file

chunks.heading: Misuse of information
chunks.summary: Know what you can and cannot share. Suppliers will sometimes ask for information they are not entitled to.
chunks.text: Procurement processes generate a range of documents and information that may be misused to gain an unfair advantage, originating from buyers or suppliers. Examples of misuse include using confidential information to help a supplier prepare bids, giving one supplier's prices to another so they can meet or beat them, and sharing information gained during negotiations with one supplier to help another. Buyer documents and information include evaluation criteria, project budget and contingency, evaluation panel members, and EOI responses; improper or untimely release may give a favoured supplier an unfair advantage. Supplier documents and information include intellectual property and commercial-in-confidence information; improper sharing with a competitor may give the competitor an unfair advantage and disadvantage the supplier in the broader market. You must maintain confidentiality and follow your agency's policies and processes for record keeping and information security. If a supplier asks which other solutions you are considering or which suppliers have been invited to respond, the correct response is to decline to provide the information because it is confidential, record details of what happened and report it, and follow your agency's policies and procedures. Suppliers may attempt to obtain information they are not entitled to, so you must know what information you can and cannot share and be aware of suppliers trying to trick you into providing information or otherwise gaining favourable treatment.
watch_outs: Naming who else was invited to respond, or revealing the budget, are the two most commonly leaked pieces of information
If a supplier fishes for information, decline, record it and report it - do not just decline and move on

chunks.heading: Improper influence, gifts and benefits
chunks.summary: Suppliers can build influence through enrichment, relationships or coercion. The safest option is to decline and declare.
chunks.text: Suppliers may attempt to improperly influence public officials to perform actions that advantage them by offering immediate or future benefits. This can involve enrichment such as gifts and benefits, relationships such as the cultivation of a friendship, and coercion such as blackmail. Examples include the offer of a bribe to influence a current procurement process, and grooming via a series of gifts to obtain favourable treatment in future contract management processes. It is easy to develop friendly relationships with suppliers or contractors, but friendships can lead to biased decision making. You must be aware of suppliers trying to develop friendships to gain influence and follow your agency's policies and procedures for managing conflicts of interest. Where a supplier on a contract you manage invites you to a personal social activity, the appropriate responses are to decline the invitation, report any attempt to improperly influence you, implement an appropriate management strategy with your manager, and declare all perceived, potential and actual conflicts of interest as per your agency's policies and procedures. Gifts and benefits are often used by suppliers to ingratiate themselves with buyers, to create a sense of friendship and of being indebted, and to incentivise and reward collusive corrupt conduct. This can result in a buyer placing unwarranted trust in a supplier and unwittingly being influenced. If you are offered gifts or benefits, think about the intent of the offer and the potential impact on you. You must follow your agency's gifts and benefits policy. The safest and easiest option is to decline and declare all gifts or benefits. Declaration is important because it helps your agency work out whether particular suppliers are systematically targeting people in your organisation.
checklist: Default to declining gifts, benefits and hospitality from suppliers
Declare the offer even when you declined it
Report any attempt at improper influence to your manager
Agree a management strategy with your manager if the relationship must continue
Keep social contact with suppliers on contracts you manage at arm's length
watch_outs: Grooming works over time through small, individually harmless gifts - declaration is what lets your agency see the pattern

chunks.heading: Your ethical obligations and how to report corruption
chunks.summary: The GSE Act sets the ethical duty; you can report internally or directly to the ICAC, with PID Act protections if you follow the requirements.
chunks.text: The Government Sector Employment (GSE) Act 2013 sets the legal requirements for all people employed in the public sector to act ethically and in the public interest. You must comply with the law and ethical obligations, follow your agency's policies and procedures, be professional and uphold the probity principles, be impartial and treat suppliers fairly and consistently, effectively manage conflicts of interest and offers of gifts and benefits, and be accountable for your decisions and actions. Reporting actual or suspected corruption helps ensure the highest ethical standards are maintained, reduces the effects of corruption by allowing it to be dealt with promptly, helps prevent future corruption because of the likelihood conduct will be reported, and is in the public interest. You do not have to prove that a matter is serious before you report it - all suspicions of corruption on reasonable grounds should be reported as soon as possible. You can report suspected corrupt conduct directly to the agency concerned, internally using your agency's internal reporting process, or directly to the NSW ICAC. Under the Public Interest Disclosures (PID) Act there are protections for NSW public officials reporting corrupt conduct. You can make a PID internally or to the ICAC, but you must comply with the PID Act to secure the associated protections. For more information on how to make a PID, consult your agency's Public Interest Disclosures policy or contact the NSW Ombudsman PID Unit.
checklist: You do not need proof or seriousness - reasonable suspicion is enough to report
Choose a route: your agency's internal reporting process, the agency concerned, or the ICAC directly
If you want PID Act protections, check your agency's PID policy first so your report meets the requirements
Contact the NSW Ombudsman PID Unit if you are unsure how to make a disclosure

chunks.heading: Councils follow a different rulebook to NSW Government agencies
chunks.summary: If you work for a council, NSW Procurement Board Directions, agency accreditation and whole-of-government contract mandates generally do not apply to you.
chunks.text: This is the single most important thing to get right. NSW local councils are not NSW Government agencies for procurement purposes. A council's procurement activities are carried out under sections 55 and 55A of the Local Government Act 1993 and Part 7 of the Local Government (General) Regulation 2021, together with the Office of Local Government's Procurement Guidelines for NSW Local Government, published July 2026, which councils must consider when setting their own procurement policy and procedures. NSW Procurement Board Directions, the agency accreditation scheme, the mandate to use whole-of-government contracts, and the enforceable procurement provisions in PBD-2019-05 are directed at NSW Government agencies, not councils. The Public Works and Procurement Regulation 2019 does deal with procurement by public bodies that are not NSW Government agencies, including councils, and councils may in some circumstances access NSW Government arrangements - but the governing obligations for a council come from the Local Government Act, not the Procurement Policy Framework. In practice councils commonly adopt the same good-practice methods that state agencies use - plan, source, manage; value for money; probity principles; evaluation plans and conduct plans - and several obligations genuinely do apply across both, notably the GIPA Act contract disclosure rules, the State Records Act, the ICAC Act, and the Modern Slavery Act. Your council will also have its own adopted procurement policy, which is the document that binds you day to day.
watch_outs: Applying NSW Government agency thresholds to a council procurement is a common and material error - the council tender threshold is $250,000 under the Local Government Act, and it is not the same rule as any state agency threshold that happens to share that number
Your council's own adopted procurement policy may set lower internal quote thresholds than the legislation requires - the policy binds you

chunks.heading: When a council must go to tender: the $250,000 threshold
chunks.summary: Section 55 requires tendering; section 55(3)(n) exempts contracts with estimated expenditure or receipt under $250,000.
chunks.text: Section 55 of the Local Government Act 1993 requires a council to invite tenders before entering into a contract. Section 55(3) lists the exemptions, and section 55(3)(n) exempts a contract involving an estimated expenditure or receipt of an amount of less than $250,000. The threshold was raised from $100,000 to $250,000 by amendments commencing in June 2019. The threshold applies to the estimated value of the contract, so estimate the whole value including options and extensions rather than a single year or a single order. Below the threshold a council is not required to tender, but the Office of Local Government encourages councils to consider using tendering, or at least a competitive quotation process, where a lesser amount is involved, in order to obtain best value. Most councils set their own internal quotation thresholds in their adopted procurement policy - for example a number of written quotes required in defined value bands - and those internal rules bind staff even though the Act does not require them.
checklist: Estimate the full contract value including all options and extension years, not the first year alone
Check whether an exemption in section 55(3) applies before assuming you must tender
Check your council's own adopted procurement policy for internal quotation thresholds below $250,000
Record the value estimate and the reasoning - it is the basis for the whole procurement method decision
watch_outs: Splitting a requirement into parts to stay under $250,000 defeats section 55 and is a serious governance failure
The threshold is about estimated value at the time of the decision, so a defensible, documented estimate matters

chunks.heading: Exemptions from council tendering under section 55(3)
chunks.summary: Several exemptions exist, including prescribed bodies such as LGP, emergencies, and a resolution-based extenuating circumstances exemption.
chunks.text: Section 55(3) of the Local Government Act 1993 sets out a number of exemptions from the requirement to invite tenders. Commonly relied-on exemptions include: a contract for goods, materials or services made with a person or body prescribed for the purpose, which is the basis on which councils can buy from arrangements established by Local Government Procurement and certain other prescribed organisations without running their own tender; a contract for the leasing or licensing of land by the council; a contract for purchase or sale by a council at public auction; a contract for the employment of a person as an employee of the council; a contract made in a case of emergency; a contract where, because of extenuating circumstances, remoteness of locality or the unavailability of competitive or reliable tenderers, the council decides by resolution stating its reasons that a satisfactory result would not be achieved by inviting tenders; and a contract involving an estimated expenditure or receipt of less than $250,000. Where an exemption depends on a council resolution, the resolution itself must state the reasons - a bare resolution is not enough. Because the exemptions are set by legislation and have been amended over time, including targeted increases for natural disaster and bushfire recovery, always check the current text of section 55(3) rather than relying on a summary before you decide not to tender.
checklist: Identify the specific paragraph of section 55(3) you are relying on, by letter
If the exemption needs a council resolution, draft the resolution so it states the reasons on its face
For a prescribed-body exemption, confirm the arrangement really was established by that body and is current
Record the exemption decision on the procurement file, with the value estimate that supports it
watch_outs: The extenuating circumstances exemption is narrow and has been tested in court - it is not a general convenience exemption
An emergency exemption relied on after the urgency has passed will not hold up

chunks.heading: Council tendering methods and the 21-day minimum
chunks.summary: Three methods under the Regulation: open tender, selective tender following an EOI advertisement, and selective tender from a recognised contractor list.
chunks.text: Part 7 of the Local Government (General) Regulation 2021 governs how councils tender. The council must decide whether tenders are to be by open tendering or selective tendering. Three methods are provided: the open tendering method, where tenders are invited by public advertisement; the selective tendering method, where invitations to tender are made following a public advertisement asking for expressions of interest; and the selective tendering method, where recognised contractors selected from a list prepared or adopted by the council are invited to tender for contracts of a particular kind. Minimum periods apply. The tender deadline must be at least 21 days after the date the advertisement is first published. Under the selective method that follows an expression of interest advertisement, the same 21-day minimum applies again when shortlisted applicants are invited to tender. The tendering provisions in Part 7 were updated by the Local Government (General) Amendment Regulation (No 2) 2022, which commenced on 16 December 2022, so check the current text rather than an older summary. Councils and joint organisations should also confirm how the provisions apply to joint procurement.
checklist: Resolve or record the decision on whether the tender is open or selective
Allow at least 21 days from first publication of the advertisement to the deadline
Under a selective process, allow another 21 days for the invitation to shortlisted applicants
Check the current Part 7 text - the tendering provisions were amended in December 2022

chunks.heading: Accepting tenders, or declining all of them
chunks.summary: A council must accept the most advantageous tender or decline all of them - and if it declines, it has four defined options.
chunks.text: Under the Local Government (General) Regulation 2021, a council must either accept the tender submission that, having regard to all the circumstances, appears to it to be the most advantageous, or decline to accept any of the tender submissions. Note the test is the most advantageous submission having regard to all the circumstances, not automatically the lowest price. If a council decides not to accept any of the tender submissions for a proposed contract, or receives no tender submissions, it must do one of the following: postpone or cancel the proposal; invite fresh tender submissions; invite fresh applications from interested persons; by resolution of the council, enter into negotiations with any person with a view to entering into a contract in relation to the subject matter of the tender; or carry out the requirements of the proposed contract itself. If the council resolves to enter into negotiations, the resolution must state the council's reasons for declining to invite fresh tender submissions or applications, and the council's reasons for determining to enter into negotiations with that person or persons.
checklist: Frame the recommendation around the most advantageous submission having regard to all the circumstances
If declining all tenders, pick one of the defined options - do not improvise a fifth
If negotiating, get a council resolution that states both sets of reasons required by the Regulation
Record the evaluation that led to the decision, whichever way it went
watch_outs: Moving into direct negotiation after a failed tender without the required resolution and reasons is a common compliance failure

chunks.heading: Buying from LGP and other prescribed arrangements
chunks.summary: LGP is prescribed under section 55, so a council can buy from an LGP-established contract above $250,000 without tendering itself.
chunks.text: Local Government Procurement has been prescribed for the purposes of section 55 of the Local Government Act 1993, which allows councils to use supply arrangements coordinated by LGP without going to tender in their own right. LGP contracts are established through a tender process in which suppliers apply to join a prequalified panel; once approved, suppliers are included on the panel and councils can engage them through the live contract. This means a council can procure goods or services from an LGP contract at values above $250,000 without running its own tender. Using a prescribed arrangement removes the tendering obligation, but it does not remove the obligation to demonstrate value for money, to run a fair and documented selection process between panel members, or to comply with your council's own procurement policy. Panels generally do not fix a single price, so a competitive request for quote between panel members is usually the right way to test value for money.
checklist: Confirm the arrangement is a current LGP or other prescribed arrangement covering what you are buying
Run a competitive quote between panel members rather than picking one - the panel does not prove value for money
Document the selection reasoning and the value for money assessment
Check your council's procurement policy for any additional internal steps

chunks.heading: Managing a kerbside collection or waste services contract
chunks.summary: Applied contract management for a council's highest-visibility service contract: what to measure, what to review, and what to escalate.
chunks.text: Kerbside domestic waste and recycling collection is usually a council's most visible, longest-running and most complaint-generating service contract, so contract management effort should be sized accordingly. In practice the work centres on four things. First, a standing contract management meeting rhythm with the contractor, typically monthly, working to a fixed agenda: actions carried forward, work health and safety and incidents, performance against each contract KPI supported by evidence, missed services and customer complaints, financial matters including invoices, rise and fall or indexation adjustments, variations and any abatements, upcoming operational changes such as route or calendar changes, and risks. Minutes with decisions, actions, owners and due dates are records under the State Records Act and are the evidence base if performance ever has to be enforced. Second, performance measurement against the KPIs the contract actually defines. Typical measures for a collection contract include missed collection rates per thousand services, time to rectify a missed service, complaint volumes and resolution times, contamination rates in the recycling and organics streams, bin repair and replacement turnaround, vehicle presentation and safety incidents, and reporting timeliness and accuracy. The critical test is whether you receive the data needed to measure each KPI independently rather than relying solely on the contractor's own reporting. Third, periodic review of the contract schedules so the operational annexures still match reality: the service specification, the price or rate schedule and its indexation mechanism, the KPI and reporting schedule, the vehicle and bin asset schedules, and the collection route or service area definitions. Where operations have drifted from the schedules, deal with it as a formal variation with a documented value for money and delegation assessment. Fourth, statutory and reporting obligations that sit alongside the contract: waste levy liabilities and reporting where the council is the relevant party, EPA waste data reporting, and the council's own reporting on domestic waste management charges. Domestic waste management is funded by a separate charge under the Local Government Act and must be accounted for accordingly, so keep the contract cost data in a state that supports that reporting. Note also that provisions in the Local Government Act protect council employees engaged in domestic and waste management services when those services are contracted out, so check the current requirements before any change in delivery model. Finally, the procurement of the contract itself is a section 55 tender in almost all cases given the values involved, so treat renewal planning as a multi-year exercise rather than an end-of-term task.
checklist: Run the contract meeting to a fixed agenda and issue minutes with actions, owners and due dates
Take the performance pack in advance and work through KPIs against evidence, not impressions
Check you can verify key measures independently of the contractor's own reporting
Review the service specification, rate schedule and indexation, KPI schedule, asset schedules and route definitions on a set cycle
Treat any operational drift from the schedules as a formal variation with value for money and delegation sign-off
Track complaints and missed services as trend data, not just as individual tickets
Keep waste levy, EPA reporting and domestic waste management charge data aligned with the contract cost data
Start renewal planning years ahead - a section 55 tender for a collection contract is a major exercise
watch_outs: Contamination and missed-service disputes are usually won or lost on the quality of the evidence trail from routine meetings
Informal agreement to a route or service change that is never varied leaves you unable to enforce the schedule you are actually operating to
Check the employee protection provisions in the Local Government Act before changing the delivery model for domestic waste services

chunks.heading: Council transparency, contracts register and modern slavery obligations
chunks.summary: Councils maintain a public contracts register at $150,000, and have had modern slavery reasonable-steps duties since July 2022.
chunks.text: Under section 27 of the Government Information (Public Access) Act 2009, a council must keep a register recording information about each contract with a private sector body that has, or is likely to have, a value of $150,000 (inc GST) or more. The information must be made available within 45 days of the contract becoming effective and remain available for 20 working days or until the obligations under the contract have been satisfied, whichever is the longer period. Contracts are classified as Class 1 at $150,000 or more, Class 2 where additional information is required in certain circumstances, and Class 3 where a Class 2 contract has a value of $5 million or more. Councils are not required to publish genuinely commercial-in-confidence provisions or information where there is an overriding public interest against disclosure. Separately, since 1 July 2022 councils have been required to take reasonable steps to ensure that goods and services they procure are not the product of modern slavery, and to report on those steps. The NSW Anti-slavery Commissioner's Guidance on Reasonable Steps, operative from 1 January 2024, applies to local councils among other bodies. From 1 July 2024, a council must file an online report with the Office of the Anti-slavery Commissioner within 45 days of the entry into force of any contract arising from a heightened modern slavery due diligence procurement process valued at $150,000 (inc GST) or more.
checklist: Publish Class 1, 2 and 3 contract information within 45 days of the contract becoming effective
Keep the entry available for 20 working days or until contract obligations are satisfied, whichever is longer
Apply modern slavery risk screening in procurement and keep the evidence of the reasonable steps taken
File the Anti-slavery Commissioner report within 45 days where a heightened due diligence contract of $150,000 or more takes effect

chunks.heading: The OLG Procurement Guidelines: status and how far they bind you
chunks.summary: Issued by the Office of Local Government in July 2026. They sit alongside the Act and Regulation as the sector's procurement guidance, and councils must consider them when setting their own policy.
chunks.text: The Procurement Guidelines for NSW Local Government were published by the Office of Local Government in July 2026, based on knowledge and understanding as at March 2026. They are listed by the Guidelines themselves as one of the legal instruments, policies and guidance governing council procurement, alongside the Local Government Act 1993, the Local Government (General) Regulation 2021, the Modern Slavery Act 2018, the Public Interest Disclosures Act 2022, the Government Information (Public Access) Act 2009 and the State Records Act 1998. Their reach is broader than the tendering threshold suggests. Procurements under the section 55 threshold are exempt from the legislated tendering requirements, but the principles and processes in the Guidelines generally apply to procurements of any value, and while councils may set their own policy and procedures they must consider these Guidelines when doing so. The Guidelines also state plainly that councils must comply with all legal obligations as well as any NSW Government procurement policies relevant to the local government sector, and that where a council is uncertain it should refer directly to the legislation and seek its own independent legal advice. Note on scope: the published document covers section 1 (procurement and local government) and section 2 (principles and governance). It forward-references a Source section, a Resources section, a Glossary, and supplementary guidance on order-splitting controls, which are not part of this document. For the detail of the tendering process itself, the Act and Part 7 of the Regulation remain the operative source.
checklist: Read the Guidelines alongside the Act and Part 7 of the Regulation - the Guidelines do not replace them
Apply the principles to procurements of any value, not only those over the tendering threshold
Show that the Guidelines were considered when your council's procurement policy was set or reviewed
Get your own legal advice where a requirement is unclear - the Guidelines say so explicitly
watch_outs: The published document is sections 1 and 2 only. Its Source section, Resources, Glossary and order-splitting guidance are referenced but not included, so do not treat it as the complete tendering procedure

chunks.heading: The $250,000 threshold: inclusive of GST, cumulative, and never to be split
chunks.summary: The threshold includes GST and applies to total estimated contract value, counting cumulative spend with a supplier on similar goods and services. Splitting orders or invoices to stay under it is contrary to the Act.
chunks.text: Section 55 of the Act prescribes a value threshold of $250,000 for contracts, and councils must follow the tendering requirements in Part 7 of the Regulation before entering into contracts of that value or more, unless exempt under section 55(3). The Guidelines add three points of detail that decide most real cases. First, the threshold is inclusive of goods and services tax. A contract at $240,000 excluding GST is $264,000 including it, and is over the threshold. Second, it applies to the total estimated contract value, and that expressly includes cumulative expenditure with a supplier for similar goods and services. Repeat purchases from the same supplier for similar things are counted together, not treated as separate small buys. Third, councils should not invoice split or order split to avoid tendering requirements, because such activities would be contrary to the Act. The Guidelines flag that controls to minimise the risk of order splitting will be covered in supplementary guidance. In practice this means the value estimate is a documented judgement about the whole arrangement over its life, made before the procurement method is chosen, and it is the first thing an auditor will test.

chunks.heading: What applies below $250,000
chunks.summary: Exempt from the legislated tendering requirements, but not from the principles. Councils set their own policy for this range and must consider the Guidelines when doing so.
chunks.text: Procurements under the value threshold prescribed by section 55 are exempt from the legislated tendering requirements. That is the full extent of the exemption. The principles and processes outlined throughout the Guidelines generally apply to procurements of any value, and councils may set their own policy and procedures in this respect but must consider the Guidelines when doing so. So a $40,000 purchase still has to demonstrate value for money, still has to be fair and open, still has to be probity-rich and documented, and still has to be recorded under the State Records Act. What changes below the threshold is the method, not the standard. Most councils set internal quotation requirements in value bands in their adopted procurement policy, and those internal rules bind staff even though the Act does not require them.

Apply the same principles you would above the threshold: value for money, fair competition, probity, records
Document the value for money assessment even for a small purchase

chunks.heading: The five principles of best-practice council procurement
chunks.summary: Value for money, fair and open competition, probity and transparency, innovation, and economic development/social outcomes/sustainability - applying to every procurement regardless of value.
chunks.text: The Guidelines set five principles that apply to every procurement, irrespective of the value, complexity and risk level involved: value for money; fair and open competition; probity and transparency; innovation; and economic development, social outcomes and sustainability. Note that this is a different list from the NSW Government's five procurement objectives, which a council officer may also encounter. The council list has probity and transparency as a principle in its own right, where the state list has easy to do business. On value for money, the Guidelines are direct: all procurement must demonstrate value for money; value for money does not mean obtaining and accepting the lowest price; a big picture view is required, assessing a range of factors to get the greatest total benefit for a community. On fair and open competition: councils must promote an even playing field and equal treatment for all potential suppliers, all suppliers must be treated and seen to be treated in an open, fair and transparent manner with access to the same information, and encouraging competition is itself a way of managing corruption risk. Councils should take a balanced approach between contracting with known reliable suppliers and reviewing contracts to improve accessibility for new entrants. On innovation: it can occur at any stage, councils should innovate where possible but not at the expense of other principles, and the focus should be on constant improvement. Alternate proposals in tenders may be considered, so long as risks are managed, the market has been tested for alternatives, and the alternate is submitted alongside a conforming tender that addresses the original request.

chunks.heading: Assessing value for money: the seven factors
chunks.summary: The Guidelines set out seven factors councils are encouraged to weigh: justifying the need, fitness for purpose, supplier assessment, broader objectives, total cost of ownership, timeliness and risk.
chunks.text: Each council may set its own evaluation criteria, but the Guidelines encourage assessment against seven factors, financial and non-financial. Justify the procurement need: is the procurement required, is there an alternative option, could existing assets, equipment, materials or resources be repurposed? Fit for purpose: does it meet the council's needs, considering quality, quantity, the methodology or program offered, and the cost quoted or tendered? Supplier assessment: can the supplier fulfil the requirements, considering relevant experience, performance history, capability and capacity, and the support and service provided? Broader council and government objectives: does the contract fit with wider policies and strategies, including council priorities, strategy and Community Strategic Plan targets, and economic, social, environmental and ethical objectives? Total cost of ownership: what other costs affect the procurement, what is required to maintain or operate it beyond the initial purchase price, what are the re-sale options, and are costs lump sum, schedule of rates, provisional or milestone-based? Timeliness: when is it needed, and what are the key dates and timeframe considerations? Risk: what uncertainties may affect or arise from the procurement, what controls apply, and what insurance cover is required?

chunks.heading: The seven key aspects of probity for councils
chunks.summary: Impartiality and fairness, defensible records, managing conflicts, confidentiality, disputes and misconduct, integrity and risk, and general compliance - aligned to the Model Code of Conduct.
chunks.text: Probity for councils means complete honesty and integrity in a process that can be confirmed and evidenced to observers: demonstrating integrity, accountability and fairness in a way that withstands external scrutiny. It is evidenced through procurement procedures that align with the Guidelines and comply with the Model Code of Conduct for Local Councils in NSW. The Guidelines set out seven key aspects. Impartiality and fairness: treat all suppliers fairly and consistently, give every market participant the same information at the same time, give submissions fair and equal consideration in accordance with the tender documents and conditions of tendering, develop probity plans and evaluation processes upfront, only approach the market with the intention, capacity and funding to execute a contract, never engage in collusive practices or give improper advantages, and put multiple staff on higher risk or higher value processes. Defensible documents and record keeping: full and clear documentation of the process, requirements, timelines, submission conditions, evaluation criteria, participation, delegation and decisions, all saved to document management systems for audit, future reference and GIPA Act purposes. Managing conflicts of interest: implement a policy, document and treat every conflict for each project, and comply with conflict of interest obligations. Confidentiality: control arrangements to protect confidential information, including legally binding confidentiality or non-disclosure clauses. Management of disputes and misconduct: a dispute resolution mechanism, a way to report misconduct or make a public interest disclosure, and management of corruption and lobbying risks. Integrity and mitigating risks: a probity plan for all phases of high-risk projects, including delivery of the contract. General compliance with all other legal and policy obligations. The Guidelines are blunt about accountability: each person involved in the procurement process is accountable for ensuring probity.
checklist: Give every market participant the same information at the same time
Write the probity plan and evaluation process before approaching the market
Only go to market when you have the intention, capacity and funding to actually award
Put more than one staff member on higher risk or higher value processes
Document the process, criteria, delegations and decisions into the records system
Document and treat every conflict of interest, for each project separately
Put confidentiality or non-disclosure terms in place for confidential information
Provide a dispute resolution mechanism and a way to report misconduct or make a PID
Run a probity plan across all phases of a high-risk project, including contract delivery
watch_outs: Going to market without the funding or intention to award is a probity breach in itself
Records exist for audit, future reference and GIPA - a decision you cannot evidence is a decision you cannot defend

chunks.heading: Probity advisers and auditors: which one, and when
chunks.summary: Five triggers for engaging one, the difference between an adviser and an auditor, and the rule that neither removes the council's own accountability.
chunks.text: It may be appropriate to engage a probity adviser or auditor if the procurement process is complex or high-risk, the project is vulnerable to corrupt practices, the project has a high level of public interest or scrutiny, there may be perceived bias or favouritism, or the integrity of the process could be questioned. Councils should include the threshold of risk that triggers this involvement in their risk management framework, so the decision is made against a standard rather than case by case. The two roles are different. A probity adviser provides advice on probity matters and acts as part of the procurement team through key phases of the lifecycle; they can help resolve probity issues as they arise, and may be engaged to oversee just the procurement process or the contract for its life. A probity auditor acts separately from the procurement team, checks whether the procurement complied with probity obligations, and generally reviews the detail after the procurement has concluded. Using an external probity adviser or auditor should be the exception and not the rule, and engagement is subject to each council's own policy and procedures. They are not a substitute for good probity and governance practices, and they do not remove the ultimate accountability for probity from the council. Where a council does engage one, it may use the Legal Services or Internal Audit and Management Contract specified by Local Government Procurement, or the NSW Government's Performance and Management Services Scheme - and if using that scheme, the council must comply with the rules associated with its use under section 55(3)(g) of the Act.

chunks.heading: Segregation of duties: the four separations
chunks.summary: At a minimum, different staff must handle supplier selection, contract drafting versus authorisation, purchase orders versus payment approval, and requesting versus receipting.
chunks.text: Ensuring clear operational separation between staff responsible for each phase of a procurement is crucial for minimising risk. Without it, transparency is limited and the council is more exposed to unethical behaviour, potential fraud and corruption. The Guidelines set a minimum: different staff are to be responsible for supplier selection activities, specifically establishing the evaluation criteria against which potential suppliers are to be assessed and evaluating submissions and recommending suppliers; drafting contract terms and authorising the final agreement; raising purchase orders and approving corresponding payments; and purchasing activities, specifically requesting and receipting delivery of goods and services, approving the expenditure of relevant funds in line with approved budget provisions, and financial delegation of authority thresholds. Councils should regularly review staff responsibilities, competence and skill development, liaising with internal teams to identify each type of risk and ensure systems manage the exposure. This is the control that small councils find hardest, because one person often covers several roles - which is exactly why the review, and a documented compensating control where full separation is impossible, matters.

Separate drafting contract terms from authorising the final agreement
Separate raising a purchase order from approving the corresponding payment
Separate requesting goods from receipting their delivery
Review responsibilities regularly, and document a compensating control wherever full separation is not possible

chunks.heading: Delegations, and the tender decision that cannot be delegated
chunks.summary: A decision to accept a tender to outsource services currently provided by council staff cannot be delegated - it must be a resolution of the council.
chunks.text: The Act provides that a council may, by resolution, delegate certain functions to its general manager or any other person or body, not including another employee of the council, and the general manager may in turn subdelegate to staff and others. There is a specific and important exception: decisions to accept tenders to provide services currently provided by members of staff of the council - that is, decisions to outsource services currently provided in-house - cannot be delegated and must be made by a resolution of the council, under section 377(1)(i) of the Act, and section 397K of the Regulation for joint organisations. Councils and the general manager should clearly document which functions of the tendering process are delegated, any limitations based on financial amount or resourcing impact, and to whom or to which position the delegation is made. Each council must review all its delegations during the first 12 months of each term of office, under section 380 of the Act. Well-implemented delegations save cost while minimising the risk of fraud, corruption or errors from inappropriate approval of transactions, and increase the efficiency of authorisation within approved budget provisions.
checklist: Check whether the tender would outsource services currently provided by council staff - if so it must go to a council resolution and cannot be delegated
Document which tendering functions are delegated, with any financial or resourcing limits
Name the person or position holding each delegation
Review all delegations within the first 12 months of each term of office
watch_outs: Accepting an outsourcing tender under delegation instead of by council resolution is a clear breach of s 377(1)(i)

chunks.heading: The tender record: everything a council must be able to produce
chunks.summary: A full list of what the tendering file must contain, with the Regulation sections behind each, from the decision to tender through to notifying tenderers of the outcome.
chunks.text: In conducting the tendering process councils should maintain full records of the entire process. The Guidelines list what that means: the council's decision to tender, or an approved procurement plan or sourcing strategy; a copy of the public advertisement or means of advertising, such as the e-tender notice or newspaper advertisement; a complete copy of the tender documents provided to tenderers; the policy, procedure and relevant plans regarding the operation of the tender evaluation panel, including the tender evaluation plan with its methodology, criteria and weightings, and the names of the staff involved; a copy of any variation to the tender documents, which should be in the form of an addendum; the names of all parties who received tender documents; a record of all subsequent dealings with tenderers and information provided to them; the names of all tenders submitted; where the council itself submits a tender, any policy or procedure on managing in-house tenders and the names of the staff involved; a record of any amendments to the tender documents and who was informed of them, under section 170(4) of the Regulation; a record of any extension or shortening of the tender period, under sections 171 and 172; a record of any variations, including clarifications, to tenders made under section 176; the evaluation of tenders and the reasons for recommending and selecting the successful tender, or for not accepting any of them, under section 178; and the notification to all tenderers of the outcome, under section 179. Councils should also document policies, procedures and decisions on risk assessment and management, comprehensively document all communications with potential tenderers, separately document the recommendation, review and final approval phases so the process is transparent and compliant with delegations, prepare an evaluation report on each tender, prepare a final report giving the reasons based on the tender criteria for the selection or for accepting none, and retain complete records of all tenders, evaluations and the contract itself.

chunks.heading: Contract records across the life of the arrangement
chunks.summary: Seven stages a council's contract records should cover, from initiation through to reporting - and the confidentiality controls that sit over all of them.
chunks.text: Good contract and records management systems help councils organise and maintain contract records, track and monitor executed contracts and contract expenditure, and reduce risk through clear reporting and alerts. The Guidelines set out the stages the records should cover. Initiation: the needs, goals and expectations. Creation: version tracking, through clarification of terms. Approval: ensuring alignment with the initiation and other requirements. Execution: signatures of the delegated persons who can sign contracts, and implementation of agreed terms through a contract management plan. Monitoring and management: ongoing monitoring and auditing of contractor performance and compliance, with deviations from contract terms addressed or handled through variation approvals. Renewal or termination: review of performance and KPIs against the terms and against council needs, goals and expectations for renewal, or documentation of the termination process and reasons in line with the contract terms. Reporting: supplier conformance, and changes to contract requirements or to the needs, goals and expectations for any future tender for the continued requirement. Over all of this sit the confidentiality obligations: information that is intellectual property, proprietary, commercial-in-confidence or otherwise confidential must not be disclosed or made accessible without suitable arrangements in place, including protection from cyber-security breach or attack.

Creation: track versions and record how terms were clarified
Approval: show the contract still matches what was initiated

Monitoring: record performance, compliance, and how deviations were addressed or varied
Renewal or termination: record the performance and KPI review, or the termination reasons
Reporting: record supplier conformance and any change in requirements for the next cycle

chunks.heading: Buying ICT, systems and AI services: the checks that apply regardless of cost
chunks.summary: Systems and platforms must go through cyber and architectural review, vendor risk assessment, AI risk consideration, privacy and data sovereignty checks, incident response terms and secure decommissioning - whatever they cost.

chunks.heading: Local preference policies, and the tension they create
chunks.summary: Councils may prefer local suppliers, but must define what local means, acknowledge the conflict with whole-of-life value for money, and state how they balance the two.
chunks.text: Procurement policies can reflect a council's local circumstances, such as an objective to support local small to medium enterprises and regional businesses, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander businesses, Australian made or developed goods or services, local innovation, Australian Disability Enterprises, social enterprises, or other economic and environmental development goals. Many councils see local businesses as integral to their communities and want public money spent within the communities they serve. But value for money and fair and open competition must still be upheld as part of a transparent and probity-rich process. The hardest part is definitional. Local has traditionally been defined by business location or employment opportunities, but even a locally based business may not keep the economic benefit in the area, because of ownership, where employees or the head office reside, or where the goods are sourced. Councils could use the local regions or communities defined in their Community Strategic Plan to provide a hierarchy for what local means. Councils should also be mindful of contractual arrangements that place onerous financial burdens on smaller or local suppliers and restrict them from tendering - contracts requiring the purchase of machinery or other upfront costs over a short timeframe can discourage local suppliers or put them at a disadvantage. To manage the tension, councils should clearly define what local means in their context, acknowledge the potential conflict between local support and life-cycle value for money, and explicitly state how they will balance these priorities in their procurement policies.
checklist: Define what local means for your council, ideally using the regions or communities in your CSP
Acknowledge in the policy that local preference can conflict with whole-of-life value for money
State explicitly how the council balances the two
Check your contract terms do not impose upfront costs that shut smaller local suppliers out
Keep fair and open competition intact - a local preference is not a reason to narrow the field improperly
watch_outs: A locally based business does not guarantee local economic benefit - ownership, head office and supply sources all matter
Onerous upfront contract requirements can exclude the local suppliers a preference policy was meant to help
