chunks.heading: Social enterprises, Aboriginal businesses and ADEs for councils
chunks.summary: For councils, an Aboriginal business is majority (51%) Aboriginal owned - a different figure from the NSW Government policy - and no open tender is required to buy from an approved disability employment organisation.
chunks.text: Councils are encouraged, though not required, to support positive social, environmental and economic outcomes in their procurements where supplier options are available. Social enterprises are businesses that trade with the goal of achieving social and environmental outcomes benefiting the public, community and environment while addressing societal problems; they may benefit disadvantaged Australians through training and employment, community and social services, or ethical products, with a significant portion of profits reinvested into social causes. On Aboriginal businesses, note the figure carefully: the Guidelines state that the NSW Government identifies an Aboriginal business as one that is majority Aboriginal ownership (51%) and is recognised through an appropriate organisation such as Supply Nation, BuyNSW, the NSW Indigenous Chamber of Commerce, or the Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations. This differs from the 50 per cent figure used in the NSW Government's Aboriginal Procurement Policy that applies to state agencies, so a council should work to the figure in the guidance it is actually bound to consider, and check the current text of both before relying on either. Councils are encouraged to identify Aboriginal businesses within their local areas, may adapt the NSW Government's Aboriginal Procurement Policy to promote opportunities and economic participation while progressing Close the Gap, or may engage Aboriginal businesses through Local Government Procurement's First Nations Procurement Scheme. Australian Disability Enterprises are not-for-profits employing people living with a disability, operating across hospitality, retail, manufacturing, recycling and horticulture. Importantly, an open tender process is not required when procuring from a person or body approved as a disability employment organisation under the Public Works and Procurement Act 1912, under section 55(3)(q) of the Act. On environmental credentials, relevant organisations may hold environmental ISO or AS standards, meet Australian National Packaging Standards and targets, operate circular economies or product impact reporting schemes, hold energy efficiency ratings or decarbonisation and Net Zero commitments, or protect biodiversity and habitat; councils are pointed to the 10Rs framework of a circular economy for extending product lifecycles.

chunks.heading: Modern slavery: reasonable steps, model clauses and annual reporting
chunks.summary: Councils must take reasonable steps at every phase, use the Anti-slavery Commissioner's model tender and contract clauses, remediate any instances found, and report annually under s 428(4).
chunks.text: Section 438ZE of the Local Government Act requires councils to take reasonable steps to ensure that goods, materials and services procured by and for the council are not the product of modern slavery within the meaning of the Modern Slavery Act 2018. The Guidelines are specific about what that involves: councils must undertake supplier due diligence throughout the procurement process to identify and manage modern slavery risks, and must remediate any instances of modern slavery. The steps should be taken at each phase of the plan, source, manage lifecycle and might include early market engagement to understand how best to integrate modern slavery risk into the sourcing process; incorporating modern slavery management criteria into prequalification schemes; including the NSW Anti-slavery Commissioner's Model Tender Clauses in tender processes; tailored due diligence to identify the residual risks associated with specific suppliers; and incorporating the Commissioner's Model Contract Clauses in supplier agreements. On reporting, the Act requires a council to publish in its annual report a statement of the action taken in relation to any issue raised by the Anti-slavery Commissioner during the year concerning the council's operations and identified as a significant issue, under section 428(4)(c), and of the steps taken to ensure goods, materials and services procured by and for the council during the year were not the product of modern slavery, under section 428(4)(d). Councils must also submit this information to the Office of the Anti-slavery Commissioner via the online form on its website. The council's procurement policy should express its commitment to addressing modern slavery risks through a public statement of policy approved by its senior governing body.

Put modern slavery management criteria into any prequalification scheme you run
Use the Anti-slavery Commissioner's Model Tender Clauses in tender processes
Use the Model Contract Clauses in supplier agreements

Remediate any instance of modern slavery you find - identification alone is not compliance

Submit the information to the Office of the Anti-slavery Commissioner via its online form
Have a public modern slavery policy statement approved by the senior governing body

chunks.heading: Code of conduct, conflicts of interest and the register of interests
chunks.summary: Pecuniary and non-pecuniary conflicts defined, ICAC's four recommendations, and a register of all disclosed conflicts across procurement activities.
chunks.text: Council staff involved in procurement must comply with the same ethical and behavioural standards as other council officials, including the council's adopted code of conduct. Concerns about breaches by staff must be reported to the general manager, or in the case of breaches by the general manager, to the mayor, as required by the Procedures for the Administration of the Model Code of Conduct. Conflicts of interest can arise at any phase and are either pecuniary or non-pecuniary. A person has a pecuniary conflict where they stand to gain or lose financially from a decision on the matter. They have a non-pecuniary conflict where a reasonable and informed person would perceive they could be influenced by a private interest in carrying out their duties. Council officials and third parties acting on behalf of councils, including suppliers engaged during the procurement process, must ensure they have no real or perceived bias or conflicts that could influence how they exercise their functions. If a conflict is identified it must be promptly declared, assessed and addressed, and if necessary alternative working arrangements or other actions should be implemented to resolve it in favour of the public interest. ICAC recommends councils implement a conflicts of interest policy; identify, disclose and manage all conflicts, which may involve a council-prepared conflict of interest management plan; encourage officials to report any conflict they believe on reasonable grounds to be undisclosed, inadequately or wrongly disclosed, or inadequately managed; and oblige suppliers and tenderers to disclose in writing any actual or potential conflicts, including relationships or interests with council staff, other tenderers and associated entities. The Model Code of Conduct prescribes mandatory requirements for disclosing and managing both kinds of conflict. Councils should keep a register of all conflicts of interest disclosed by staff and by representatives of contracted entities for all procurement activities, which helps ensure conflicts are declared and managed as they arise and assists in managing conflicts in any subsequent procurement with that supplier. Section 8B of the Act requires sound financial management, and councils must implement and regularly review financial controls and budgetary processes for procurement.

Report code of conduct breaches to the general manager, or to the mayor if the breach is by the general manager

chunks.heading: Procurement resourcing, specialist teams and training
chunks.summary: Seven questions for reviewing whether procurement resourcing is adequate, and the training topics councils should audit staff against.
chunks.text: Procurement staff duties vary with the size of the council, the staff available and the complexity and number of procurement activities, but all staff undertaking procurement play a crucial role in ensuring value for money and meeting the council's needs. Councils should regularly review whether procurement resources are adequate and appropriate, considering: the requirements for achieving the council's goals in its Community Strategic Plan and Operational Plan; who the go-to person or team for procurement support is; what their primary responsibilities are, which may include procedural advice, researching suppliers and options, drafting documentation, tendering, executing purchase agreements, and ensuring products meet standards and comply with legislation; whether that person or team has the right knowledge and skills or needs additional training, and whether training can be coordinated with other councils or done online to reduce cost; whether a specialist person or team is essential and appropriate for the council's size and needs; which service model - decentralised, centre-led or centralised - best suits the council; and whether external expertise is needed. A specialist team can reduce costs, streamline processes and improve outcomes, and improves efficiency by understanding council spending and consolidating purchasing, building relationships with internal groups such as finance, project management, marketing, design and engineering, with other councils and joint organisations, and with suppliers, and by identifying opportunities such as joint procurement with other councils to maximise purchasing power. Where a council lacks in-house expertise it may engage external professionals, but must ensure systems protect confidentiality, provide adequate oversight of their work and approvals, and mitigate risks - and that engagement is itself subject to the Act and Regulation depending on cost and risk. Councils should audit staff to assess the knowledge and skills mix across the procurement lifecycle and train to close gaps.

Identify the go-to person or team and what they are actually responsible for

Consider whether a specialist team suits the council's size and complexity
Choose a service model deliberately: decentralised, centre-led or centralised
Look for joint procurement opportunities with other councils and joint organisations
Where external expertise is engaged, put confidentiality, oversight and risk controls in place

chunks.heading: Audit, risk framework and reporting corrupt conduct
chunks.summary: Every council must have an Audit, Risk and Improvement Committee; risk management must be proportionate, with the policy setting the trigger for a full risk plan.
chunks.text: All councils are required to appoint an Audit, Risk and Improvement Committee, which must review aspects of the council's operations including compliance, risk management, fraud and corruption control, financial management and governance. Including an audit of the council's procurement practices in the internal audit work plan, linked to strategic objectives, helps identify and mitigate current and emerging risks. Councils with larger procurement budgets, diverse or complex arrangements and higher risks may need more frequent general reviews of procurement policies and processes in addition to an audit; this may not be necessary for smaller councils with lower risk profiles. On risk generally, all procurement carries some level of risk, including heightened risk of fraud and corruption at any phase and throughout the contract's duration, and modern slavery risk must be managed before entering and during the life of the contract. Councils should develop a risk management framework, and may refer to ISO 31000:2018 Risk Management - Guidelines for general guidance. Risk management practices should be proportionate to value and risk level: a simple mechanism may suffice for low value, low risk procurement, while high value and high-risk procurement needs a more structured plan including consideration of probity. A council's procurement policy should establish the trigger point for when a more complex risk management plan is necessary. On corrupt conduct, council staff involved in procurement must remain vigilant for behaviour that may indicate corrupt conduct as defined in the Independent Commission Against Corruption Act 1988. Councils must ensure staff are aware that suspected corrupt conduct can be reported directly to the ICAC, and that suppliers understand how to report concerns - whether to the ICAC, a designated council officer, or through the council's public interest disclosures policy - which could be addressed through a statement of business ethics for suppliers.
checklist: Put procurement into the internal audit work plan, linked to strategic objectives
Build a risk management framework - ISO 31000:2018 is the reference the Guidelines name
Scale risk treatment to value and risk: simple for low, structured plus probity for high
Set the trigger point in the procurement policy for when a full risk plan is required
Make sure staff know they can report suspected corrupt conduct directly to the ICAC
Tell suppliers how to raise concerns - a statement of business ethics is the Guidelines' suggestion
Manage modern slavery risk before entering the contract and throughout its life

chunks.heading: Plan, source, manage for councils: what each phase involves
chunks.summary: The council version of the three-phase lifecycle, with the specific activities and artefacts the Guidelines name for each.
chunks.text: The plan, source, manage approach describes the lifecycle phases of most typical procurements. Every phase matters, but councils need not spend the same time and resources on each, and should assess based on the size of the activity, the level of risk and complexity, and their own situation and needs. Risk management strategies should be in place at each phase, and a whole-of-life risk-based approach should be taken to supplier and product due diligence, with the Guidelines pointing councils to ICAC's guidance on supplier due diligence. Methodologies and decisions throughout the lifecycle should be documented and filed under the State Records Act and the council's recordkeeping policy, to ensure transparency and accountability and to demonstrate defensible processes and decision-making. Plan involves a needs analysis such as a master plan, project plan or business case; determining availability of funds through budgetary requests, grants and approvals; developing procurement documents that clearly articulate requirements and terms, such as the scope, specification and statement of requirements; identifying risk and management measures through a risk assessment with controls and treatments; understanding community and other stakeholder needs and expectations, including outcomes of community engagement, council resolutions or stakeholder consultation; market analysis and early industry engagement to test appetite to supply, capacity, capability, factors influencing supply and innovation, through requests for information or expressions of interest; and formalising the procurement strategy through a procurement plan, communications plan, evaluation plan and finalised RFT or RFQ and contract documents. Source involves approaching the market by advertising requests with conditions of participation; selecting suppliers that pass due diligence checks, address selection and evaluation criteria and best demonstrate value for money through a scoring methodology; clarifying terms, recommending and awarding a contract via selection or recommendation reports for delegated approvers; debriefing unsuccessful proponents through post-tender review or feedback meetings; and contract disclosure in compliance with legislation, by displaying awarded contract details on the contracts register. Manage involves buyer and supplier documenting agreed systems, processes, risks and responsibilities in a contract management plan; ensuring a smooth transition of services, such as a transition plan for a new supplier; ensuring governance and management of contractual obligations, including milestone-based billing and management and approval of variations; tracking supplier performance and delivery against the contract management plan and terms; considering strategy for any renewal, extension or variation; and reviewing processes, outcomes, documentation, records and supplier performance to inform future procurements, through a post contract review report.
checklist: Plan: needs analysis, funding, requirements documents, risk assessment, stakeholder and community input, market analysis, documented strategy
Source: approach the market with conditions of participation, run due diligence and scored evaluation, recommend and award, debrief unsuccessful proponents, disclose the contract
Manage: contract management plan, transition plan, variation and billing governance, performance tracking, renewal strategy, post contract review
Scale the effort at each phase to size, risk and complexity
Keep risk strategies and supplier due diligence running across all three phases
File methodologies and decisions under the State Records Act and your recordkeeping policy

chunks.heading: Registering to sell to NSW Government
chunks.summary: Register on the buy.nsw Supplier Hub with a valid ABN, then keep the profile current so buyers can find you.
chunks.text: To sell to the NSW Government you must be a registered business with an Australian Business Number. Registration is on the buy.nsw Supplier Hub: create an account and complete your profile. Registering and creating a profile lets NSW Government buyers find you on the supplier list, allows you to be matched with opportunities based on your profile, and lets you apply for contracts and schemes. Registration of NSW Government suppliers on the Supplier Hub has been mandated by Procurement Board Direction. When you complete your profile you can add business identifiers. These are either self-identified, shown in blue, or verified through a third party, shown in green - for example verified Aboriginal owned business, disability employment organisation, verified social enterprise, or gender equitable employer. Verified identifiers carry much more weight with buyers than self-declared ones, because several policies depend on recognised status. Small businesses with fewer than 20 full-time equivalent employees should also register for NSW Government Faster Payment Terms, which is what triggers the 5 business day payment obligation on invoices between $10,000 and $1 million. Separately, NSW eTendering is where tenders are advertised and managed, where quotes are requested from suppliers on prequalification schemes, and where awarded contracts over $150,000 (inc GST) are published.
keywords: how do i sell to government
checklist: Have a current ABN before you start
Create your Supplier Hub account and complete the whole profile, not just the minimum fields
Get your identifiers verified rather than self-declared where you are eligible
If you have fewer than 20 FTE, register as a small business so the 5-day payment terms apply
Set up notifications for the categories and schemes you want to hear about
Keep insurances, licences and capability statements current in the profile
watch_outs: An incomplete or stale profile is the most common reason capable suppliers never get found by buyers doing market analysis

chunks.heading: Finding opportunities, and the thresholds that work in your favour
chunks.summary: Not every opportunity is advertised. Below several thresholds a buyer can come straight to you if you are the right kind of supplier.
chunks.text: Advertised tenders on NSW eTendering are only part of the picture. A large share of government spend flows through whole-of-government contracts, prequalification schemes and direct engagement below certain thresholds, so being findable and being on the right scheme often matters more than watching the tender feed. Direct engagement thresholds that work in a supplier's favour include: under $10,000, a NSW Government agency can buy from any supplier; up to $50,000, an agency can buy directly from a small business with fewer than 20 FTE even if the item is on a whole-of-government contract; under $150,000, an agency can buy directly from a regional supplier; up to $250,000, an agency must give first consideration to an Aboriginal business recognised through an appropriate organisation, and can buy directly from an Aboriginal business or an SME; up to $3 million, the SME and Regional Procurement Policy requires first preference to SMEs for direct purchases, including from panels and schemes; and there is no value limit on buying from approved disability employment organisations via a single written quote. For councils, the equivalent access point is the $250,000 tendering threshold under the Local Government Act plus each council's own quotation thresholds, and panels established by Local Government Procurement. Practical implication: make sure the buyer can tell, from your registered profile, which of these categories you fall into.
keywords: how do i get on a panel
checklist: Set up eTendering notifications for your categories
Identify which prequalification schemes cover what you sell and apply to join
Make your SME, regional, Aboriginal, social enterprise or ADE status visible and verified
For council work, watch individual council tender pages and consider LGP panels
Introduce yourself to category buyers - market analysis is a real stage and buyers do look

chunks.heading: Writing a competitive response
chunks.summary: Buyers score against a published set of criteria using a scoresheet. Write to those criteria, evidence every claim, and answer the mandatory conditions first.
chunks.text: Buyers evaluate in a defined order: first they rule out responses that fail the tender conditions or the mandatory criteria, then they score the remaining responses against the published non-mandatory criteria using an evaluation plan finalised before the tender closed. That order tells you how to write. Deal with the mandatory criteria and conditions of participation explicitly and early, in the buyer's own words, so nobody has to hunt for compliance. Use the response template provided; buyers use it precisely so responses are comparable, and departing from it makes you harder to score. Write to each published criterion in turn rather than submitting generic capability material. Evidence every claim - buyers are required to verify that suppliers have provided truthful information about skills, experience, business records and qualifications, so a claim you cannot evidence is a liability rather than an asset. Address capability and capacity separately: capability is the right skills, qualifications, experience, licences and insurances, capacity is having sufficient time, staff, equipment, materials and other resources to actually deliver. Price is scored against a stated weighting alongside non-price factors, so the lowest price does not automatically win, and the buyer's task is fitness for purpose at the lowest whole-of-life cost. If the procurement is over $3 million, expect mandatory minimum non-price criteria on SME and regional participation. Ask questions through the official channel during the tender period: your question will be deidentified and the answer circulated to all respondents, which is normal and does not disadvantage you. Do not expect leniency on lateness - buyers should not accept late submissions unless they caused the delay or no other bidder is disadvantaged.
checklist: Answer the mandatory criteria and conditions of participation first, explicitly
Use the buyer's response template and their headings
Write to each published criterion separately - do not submit a generic capability statement
Evidence every claim with a reference, a certificate, a named project or a number
Cover capability and capacity as two different things
Ask clarification questions through the official channel, early
Submit well before the deadline - closing time is typically 3pm and late bids are usually rejected
watch_outs: Failing a single mandatory criterion removes you before any of your strengths are read
Overstating experience is checked at due diligence and can end the engagement

chunks.heading: Getting paid, and what to do when you are not
chunks.summary: Registered small businesses are entitled to 5 business day payment on correctly rendered invoices between $10,000 and $1 million.
chunks.text: If you are a registered small business with fewer than 20 full-time equivalent employees, a NSW Government agency must pay your correctly rendered invoices between $10,000 and $1 million within 5 business days under the Faster Payment Terms Policy. Invoices under $10,000 should be paid as soon as possible, ideally instantly by purchasing card. If you subcontract to a large business that holds a NSW Government goods and services contract over $7.5 million, that head contractor must pay you within 20 business days of a correctly rendered invoice under the Small Business Shorter Payment Terms Policy. The phrase correctly rendered does real work here: the payment clock does not start until the invoice meets the requirements set out in the contract or purchase order, so confirm at the outset exactly what the buyer needs on the invoice, and always quote the purchase order number. The Office of the Small Business Commissioner monitors and reports on agency payment performance to small businesses, and agencies must report their on-time payment record in their annual report. If payment is late, start with the contract manager and the agency's accounts payable, then escalate through the agency's complaints process; the NSW Small Business Commissioner is the external avenue for small business payment disputes.
keywords: how long until i get paid
checklist: Register your small business status so the 5-day terms apply
Confirm in writing what makes an invoice correctly rendered for this contract
Always include the purchase order number
If payment is late, contact the contract manager and accounts payable in writing first
Escalate through the agency's complaints process, then to the NSW Small Business Commissioner if unresolved

chunks.heading: Debriefs and complaints when you are unsuccessful
chunks.summary: You can ask for a debrief - SMEs and regional suppliers can require one. Complaints split into covered and general procurement complaints.
chunks.text: After a contract is awarded, buyers should debrief unsuccessful suppliers, covering the strengths in your response and areas for improvement in future submissions. Agencies must provide pre and post-tender briefings when reasonably requested by SMEs and regional suppliers. A debrief is feedback, not a re-argument of the decision, and the buyer must not disclose commercial-in-confidence information such as other suppliers' responses. If you believe something went wrong with the process rather than just the outcome, NSW distinguishes two kinds of complaint. A covered procurement complaint alleges a breach of the enforceable procurement provisions in the EPP Direction, which generally apply above $680,000 (ex GST) for goods and services or $9.584 million (ex GST) for construction. Under the Public Works and Procurement Act 1912 a supplier may lodge such a complaint with the head of the government agency, and the agency head must investigate and attempt to resolve it. The NSW Procurement Board has no statutory role in covered procurement complaints - they are a matter for the agency, the supplier and, if proceedings are taken, the Supreme Court. A general procurement complaint covers everything else, including procurements below the thresholds, exempt procurements, agencies not covered by the EPP Direction, and matters outside the scope of the Direction. These are handled under the NSW Procurement Board Complaint Management Guidelines, normally starting with the agency itself. For a council procurement, complaints go through the council's own complaints process, and the NSW Ombudsman and the Office of Local Government are the external avenues. Suspected corruption goes to the ICAC in either case.
checklist: Ask for a debrief in writing promptly after the award notification
If you are an SME or regional supplier, say so - a reasonable request must be met
Separate a complaint about the process from disappointment about the outcome before you lodge
For a covered procurement, lodge with the agency head under the PWP Act
For a general complaint, follow the agency's or council's complaints process first
Report suspected corruption to the ICAC rather than through the complaints process

chunks.heading: Aboriginal businesses, social enterprises and disability employment organisations
chunks.summary: Recognition by an approved body is what unlocks the direct-engagement and first-consideration pathways.
chunks.text: For the purposes of the NSW Aboriginal Procurement Policy, an Aboriginal business is one that has at least 50 per cent Aboriginal ownership and is recognised through an appropriate organisation, such as Supply Nation, the NSW Indigenous Chamber of Commerce, or the Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations. Recognition is the gate: the first-consideration requirement for procurements up to $250,000, and the ability of an agency to buy directly at that level, depend on it. The Aboriginal Procurement Policy, which took effect in January 2021, also set a target for Aboriginal-owned businesses to be awarded at least three per cent of the total number of domestic contracts for goods and services issued by NSW Government agencies. Social enterprises tackle social problems, improve communities, provide people with access to employment and training, or help the environment. Many are small businesses, SMEs, Aboriginal businesses or Australian Disability Enterprises, and qualify for purchasing preferences. Buyers can purchase goods and services from approved disability employment organisations via a single written quote with no value limit. In every case, get the status verified on your buy.nsw Supplier Hub profile - verified identifiers appear in green and self-declared ones in blue, and policies that depend on recognised status need the verified version.
checklist: Get recognised by Supply Nation, the NSW Indigenous Chamber of Commerce or ORIC if you are an Aboriginal business
Get the identifier verified on your Supplier Hub profile, not just self-declared
Make sure buyers can see the status when they search the Supplier Hub during market analysis
Tell buyers which direct-engagement pathway applies to you - many buyers do not know the thresholds by heart

chunks.heading: What is expected of you as a supplier
chunks.summary: Corrupt conduct rules apply to suppliers too. Collusion, information fishing and gift-based influence all carry real consequences.
chunks.text: Corrupt conduct is not something only public officials can commit. It occurs when a member of the public influences, or tries to influence, a public official to use their position in a way that is dishonest or partial, and when the actions of any person impair or could impair public confidence in public administration - which expressly includes collusive tendering and dishonestly obtaining or benefiting from public funds or assets for private advantage. In practical terms, three supplier behaviours regularly cause problems. Collusion between suppliers to artificially elevate prices or to manipulate which of them wins the work. Fishing for information a buyer is not entitled to give you, such as which other suppliers were invited, the budget, or another supplier's pricing - buyers are trained to decline, record and report these requests. And influence-building through gifts, hospitality or cultivated friendships, which buyers are trained to decline and declare. Buyers are also required to verify that you have provided truthful information about your skills, experience, business records and qualifications, so overstating capability is checked rather than assumed. The Risk and Compliance Subcommittee of the NSW Procurement Board deals with remedial action for poor supplier performance or behaviour, and suppliers are members of the public whose confidence in the system the government is obliged to maintain.
watch_outs: Asking a buyer who else is bidding puts you on a written record as having sought information you are not entitled to
Overstated credentials are checked at due diligence, and the failure is discovered at the worst possible time

chunks.heading: The five categories of due diligence check
chunks.summary: Due diligence answers one question - should we be doing business with this supplier - across five categories of check.
chunks.text: In a nutshell, due diligence helps to answer the question: should we be doing business with this supplier? Numerous ICAC investigations have shown that poor due diligence has led to corrupt conduct. Conducting supplier due diligence helps you ensure value for money, prevent corrupt conduct, maintain trust in public administration and comply with legal and regulatory expectations. Ensuring that suppliers are legitimate and capable of delivering the goods or services specified in your contract is your responsibility. The ICAC's Supplier Due Diligence guide organises checks into five categories, framed as questions. Is the supplier genuine - does the business actually exist as claimed, and is it who it says it is? Is the supplier capable and reliable - can they actually do this work, and have they done it before? Is the supplier financially viable - can they survive the length of the contract? Do they have the required authorities, licences and status - the specific legal permissions the work requires? Are they of good repute and integrity - is there history that should give you pause? The guide covers what due diligence is, why, when and how it should be performed, and by whom, and includes practical techniques for probing the integrity of online suppliers, such as viewing webpage source code, searching internet archives, obtaining a site's IP address and geolocation, and reverse image searches.
checklist: Genuine: verify the ABN against the Australian Business Register and check it matches the entity name you are contracting with
Capable and reliable: check referees, past performance and comparable projects rather than accepting the claim
Financially viable: assess whether the business can survive the contract term, proportionate to the value and duration
Authorities and licences: verify each licence, registration and insurance directly with the issuing body, and check currency
Repute and integrity: search for adverse findings, regulator actions and litigation history
Scale the depth of checking to the value, duration and risk of the engagement

chunks.heading: Supplier red flags
chunks.summary: ABN problems, no separation between ownership and management, and thin verifiable history are the signals ICAC highlights.
chunks.text: Red flags include suppliers that have no ABN, an invalid ABN, or an ABN that does not match to the Australian Business Register. ICAC's past investigations show that corruption risk is much greater where there is little or no separation between management and ownership of the company, so a sole-controlled entity bidding for significant work warrants closer attention - not disqualification, but a deeper look. Other signals worth probing include a business whose online presence is thin, recently created, or inconsistent with its claimed trading history; addresses that resolve to residential premises, virtual offices or the address of another bidder; directors or shareholders who overlap with another bidder in the same process; referees who cannot be independently located; insurance or licence certificates supplied as images rather than verifiable records; and pricing that is markedly out of line with the rest of the field in either direction. ICAC's guide includes techniques for probing the online presence of a supplier, including viewing webpage source code, searching internet archives for how long a site has really existed, obtaining a site's IP address and geolocation, and running reverse image searches on photographs used to establish credibility. The general principle is that a claim that cannot be independently verified should not be treated as verified.
checklist: Validate the ABN on the Australian Business Register and confirm the entity name matches
Look for overlap in directors, shareholders, addresses or contact details between bidders
Check how long the supplier's web presence has genuinely existed
Verify licences and insurances with the issuing body, not from a supplied image
Locate and actually contact referees independently
Treat unverifiable claims as unverified, and say so in the evaluation record
watch_outs: Two bidders sharing an address, a phone number or a director is a collusion indicator that needs escalation, not a clerical query
A very low bid can indicate a supplier who has misunderstood the scope, or who intends to recover margin through variations

chunks.heading: When to run due diligence across the procurement lifecycle
chunks.summary: Design the checks at planning, run them before engagement, and repeat them during long contracts - always on a bank detail change.
chunks.text: Due diligence is not a single gate. At the planning stage you design it: identify the capabilities the procurement genuinely requires, understand the regulatory environment applying to suppliers in that market, and decide what information suppliers must provide and how you will verify it. Write those requirements into the market-facing documents, not just the internal plan, because you can only verify what you asked for. At the sourcing stage you run the checks: after identifying potential suppliers and before finalising the engagement, verify that suppliers are capable of performing the work and have provided truthful information about their skills, experience, business records and qualifications. This applies both to individual procurements and to admitting suppliers onto a panel or prequalification scheme - a scheme is only as reliable as the checks that put suppliers on it. At the manage stage you repeat them: for lengthy contracts, re-check that insurances and licences remain current, and for more complex contracts run ongoing checks on the supplier's corporate structure, financial health and regulatory compliance. Additional due diligence is always required if the supplier requests a change to its bank account details - verify independently, through contact details you already hold, never through details supplied in the request itself.
checklist: Plan: decide what evidence is required and how it will be verified, and put it in the RFx
Source: verify before you finalise the engagement, not after
Panel entry: apply the same rigour to scheme admission as to a direct engagement
Manage: diarise insurance and licence expiries and re-check on long contracts
Always: verify any bank detail change through an independently held contact channel
